entries.content:
本章脉络

第十二章是神迹之书的结尾，也是通往荣耀之书的大门。伯大尼的膏抹（1-11节）：马利亚把极贵的香膏抹在耶稣脚上。进入耶路撒冷（12-19节）：众人拿着棕树枝喊「和散那」。希腊人求见（20-36节）：耶稣说「人子得荣耀的时候到了」，又说一粒麦子要落在地里死了。不信与以赛亚的预言（37-43节）。最后的公开呼召（44-50节）。

从2:4「我的时候还没有到」开始，「时候」这条线在整卷书里一再出现。到了12:23，耶稣终于说：「人子得荣耀的时候到了。」引出这句话的，是几个希腊人来求见他。外邦人开始来到他面前，这是他要被「举起来、吸引万人」的信号。

深读 12:1-8 一斤极贵的香膏

1. 价值。 马利亚拿着「一斤极贵的真哪哒香膏」（12:3），哪哒香膏从印度一带进口。犹大说可以卖「三百个银币」（dēnarion），和合本译作「三十两银子」。一个银币是一个工人一天的工资，三百个银币差不多是一年的收入。

2. 抹脚，用头发擦。 一般膏抹是抹在头上（马太、马可记载她也浇在耶稣头上），约翰却只记她抹耶稣的脚，又用头发去擦。在当时的文化里，一个女人在众人面前把头发放下来，是很不寻常、甚至有失体统的举动。马利亚不顾别人的眼光，把最贵重的东西、最卑微的姿态，都献给了耶稣。「屋里就满了膏的香气」，这是约翰式的细节：她的奉献，整个屋子都闻得到。

3. 犹大的「关心穷人」。 「这香膏为什么不卖……周济穷人呢？」（12:5）约翰揭露他的动机：「他说这话，并不是挂念穷人，乃因他是个贼，又带着钱囊，常取其中所存的。」（12:6）最冠冕堂皇的批评，有时出自最自私的心。

4. 「为我安葬之日存留的」。 耶稣说：「由她吧！她是为我安葬之日存留的。」（12:7）马利亚也许并不完全明白，但她的举动预先指向了耶稣的死与安葬。六天以后，他就要被安葬，而那时尼哥德慕要带来约一百斤的没药和沉香（19:39）。

深读 12:12-16 棕树枝、和散那与驴驹

1. 棕树枝的意义。 「就拿着棕树枝出去迎接他。」（12:13）棕树枝在当时是民族胜利的象征：西门·马加比收复耶路撒冷的堡垒时（主前141年），人们就是拿着棕树枝欢呼（马加比一书13:51），后来犹太人反抗罗马时铸的钱币上也有棕树。众人迎接的，是一位他们期待能带来政治解放的王。

2. 「和散那」。 「和散那！奉主名来的以色列王是应当称颂的！」这出自诗篇118:25-26。「和散那」原是希伯来文的祷告「求你拯救」，后来成为欢呼的用语。众人喊着「求你拯救」，心里想的是脱离罗马；耶稣要成就的却是更深的拯救：救人脱离罪和神的审判，而他要借着替我们死来成就。「以色列王」这几个字不在诗篇里，是众人加上的。

3. 驴驹的回答。 耶稣「得了一个驴驹，就骑上」（12:14），应验撒迦利亚书9:9。在众人的政治期待中，耶稣用一个无声的举动回答：他是王，却是骑着驴驹、谦和的王，不是骑着战马的征服者。撒迦利亚书接着说，神「必除灭以法莲的战车」，而这位王「必向列国讲和平」（亚9:10）。

4. 「不要惧怕」。 约翰的引文是「锡安的民哪，不要惧怕！」而撒迦利亚书原文是「应当大大喜乐」。「不要惧怕」可能来自以赛亚书40:9或西番雅书3:16，而西番雅书3:15正说到「以色列的王耶和华在你中间」。约翰把几处经文合在一起，强调这位王来，带来的是安慰。

5. 门徒后来才明白。 「这些事门徒起先不明白，等到耶稣得了荣耀以后才想起这话是指着他写的。」（12:16）这和2:22一样：有些事要在十字架和复活之后，才能读懂。

深读 12:20-28「人子得荣耀的时候到了」

1. 希腊人来了。 「先生，我们愿意见耶稣。」（12:21）这些希腊人很可能是敬畏神的外邦人，上来过节礼拜。法利赛人刚刚说「世人都随从他去了」（12:19），紧接着，「世人」的代表就来了。

2. 一粒麦子。 耶稣没有直接回答见不见他们，而是说：「一粒麦子不落在地里死了，仍旧是一粒；若是死了，就结出许多子粒来。」（12:24）希腊人要「见」耶稣，但他们真正能与耶稣相遇，要等到他死了以后。十字架将打开一条路，让各国的人都能来到他面前。

3. 同样的道路。 「爱惜自己生命的，就失丧生命；在这世上恨恶自己生命的，就要保守生命到永生。」（12:25）「恨恶」是闪族语言中强烈的对比说法，意思是「两相比较，把它放在次位」，不是心理上的自我厌恶。麦子的原则不只适用于耶稣，也适用于跟随他的人。

4. 约翰福音的客西马尼。 「我现在心里忧愁，我说什么才好呢？父啊，救我脱离这时候；但我原是为这时候来的。父啊，愿你荣耀你的名！」（12:27-28）约翰福音没有记载客西马尼园的祷告，但这几句话有同样的挣扎和同样的顺服。耶稣是真实的人，他面对十字架时真实地忧愁；他也是顺服的子，他选择了父的荣耀。

5. 天上的声音。 「我已经荣耀了我的名，还要再荣耀。」（12:28）这是约翰福音里唯一一次从天上来的声音。「已经荣耀」是在耶稣的事奉和神迹中，「还要再荣耀」是在即将来临的十字架和复活中。

要点：一粒麦子的比喻，是整卷约翰福音对十字架的总结：死亡不是失败，而是结出许多子粒的唯一道路。
深读 12:31-33「我若从地上被举起来」

1. 两个「现在」。 「现在这世界受审判，这世界的王要被赶出去。」（12:31）表面上是世界审判了耶稣，其实是世界在十字架前受了审判；而罪人当受的刑罚，落在了那位替我们被举起来的人身上。「这世界的王」指撒但（14:30；16:11）。在十字架上，看起来得胜的黑暗权势，其实被赶了出去。

2. 第三次「举起来」。 「我若从地上被举起来，就要吸引万人来归我。」（12:32）约翰立刻解释：「耶稣这话原是指着自己将要怎样死说的。」（12:33）这是三次「举起来」（3:14；8:28）的最后一次，也最清楚：被钉在十字架上高高举起，同时就是被高举得荣耀。

3. 「万人」。 （有些抄本作「万物」。）在希腊人来求见的上下文中，「万人」最自然的意思是「各样的人」，不只犹太人，也包括外邦人。这呼应10:16和11:52：要把神四散的子民聚集归一。

深读 12:37-43「以赛亚因为看见他的荣耀」

1. 神迹之书的总结。 「他虽然在他们面前行了许多神迹，他们还是不信他。」（12:37）约翰在神迹之书的结尾，用两处以赛亚书来解释这个令人心碎的事实：以赛亚书53:1「我们所传的有谁信呢？」以及以赛亚书6:10（约翰引作「主叫他们瞎了眼，硬了心」，12:40）。约翰的引法明白指出，使人心刚硬的是神。

2. 「他们所以不能信」。 这句话（12:39）很沉重。约翰同时说了两件事：他们「不信」（12:37，是他们自己的拒绝），他们「不能信」（12:39，神的审判使他们的心刚硬）。圣经常常把这两者并列：人拒绝光，神就任凭他们停在黑暗里。约翰并不调和这两面：神在审判中主权地使人心刚硬（参6:44），而人仍要为拒绝光完全负责。没有一个真心要来的人会被拒之门外（6:37）。

3. 以赛亚看见了谁的荣耀？ 「以赛亚因为看见他的荣耀，就指着他说这话。」（12:41）以赛亚书6章，以赛亚看见的是「主坐在高高的宝座上」，撒拉弗喊着「圣哉！圣哉！圣哉！万军之耶和华」。约翰说，以赛亚所看见的，是耶稣的荣耀。这是约翰福音对耶稣神性最直接的宣告之一。许多学者还指出，以赛亚书6:1形容主「高高」在宝座上，与52:13说受苦的仆人「被高举上升」，用的是相近的字。约翰似乎是把两处连在一起读：宝座上的主，和被举起来的仆人，是同一位。

4. 暗中的信徒。 「虽然如此，官长中却有好些信他的，只因法利赛人的缘故，就不承认……这是因他们爱人的荣耀过于爱神的荣耀。」（12:42-43）这呼应5:44。约翰对暗中的信徒没有简单地定罪，但他清楚指出问题所在：怕失去人的称赞，也就是我们常说的「面子」。

默想

默想： 耶稣自己就是那粒落在地里死了的麦子，他为我死，好叫我成为他所结的子粒之一。马利亚的香膏，是一个蒙了大爱的人自然的回应。当我想到他为我付上的，我心里有没有一样「舍不得」的东西开始松手？我在乎人的眼光（我们常说的「面子」），是不是因为我还没有尝够从神来的荣耀？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 12 closes the Book of Signs and opens the door to the Book of Glory. The anointing at Bethany (vv. 1–11): Mary pours costly ointment on Jesus' feet. The entry into Jerusalem (vv. 12–19): the crowd waves palm branches and shouts "Hosanna." The Greeks seek Jesus (vv. 20–36): Jesus says, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified," and speaks of a grain of wheat falling into the earth and dying. Unbelief and Isaiah's prophecy (vv. 37–43). The final public appeal (vv. 44–50).

From "My hour has not yet come" in 2:4, the thread of the "hour" has run through the whole book. At 12:23 Jesus finally says, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified." What prompts it is a few Greeks asking to see him. Gentiles are beginning to come to him, the signal that he is about to be "lifted up" and "draw all people."

Going Deeper: 12:1–8 A Pound of Costly Ointment

1. The value. Mary takes "a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard" (12:3), imported from around India. Judas says it could have been sold for "three hundred denarii" (the Chinese Union Version renders this "thirty taels of silver"). A denarius was a laborer's daily wage, so three hundred was about a year's income.

2. Anointing his feet and wiping them with her hair. Anointing was usually done on the head (Matthew and Mark say she poured it on Jesus' head), but John records only that she anointed his feet and wiped them with her hair. In that culture, a woman letting down her hair in public was highly unusual, even improper. Mary ignored what others thought and gave Jesus her most precious possession in the humblest posture. "The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume": a very Johannine detail. The whole house could smell her devotion.

3. Judas's "concern for the poor." "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" (12:5). John exposes his motive: "He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it" (12:6). The most high-minded criticism sometimes comes from the most selfish heart.

4. "For the day of my burial." Jesus says, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial" (12:7). Mary may not have fully understood, but her act became a foreshadowing of Jesus' death. Six days later he would be buried, and Nicodemus would bring about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39).

Going Deeper: 12:12–16 Palm Branches, Hosanna and a Donkey's Colt

1. What palm branches meant. "So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him" (12:13). Palm branches were then a symbol of national victory. When Simon Maccabeus took the Jerusalem citadel (141 BC), people celebrated with palm branches (1 Maccabees 13:51), and coins minted later during the Jewish revolts against Rome bore palm trees. The crowd was welcoming a king they hoped would bring political liberation.

2. "Hosanna." "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" comes from Psalm 118:25–26. "Hosanna" was originally a Hebrew prayer, "Save, please!", which became a shout of acclaim. The crowd cried "save us," thinking of rescue from Rome; Jesus was about to accomplish a far deeper salvation: rescue from sin and God's judgment, won by dying in our place. "Even the King of Israel" isn't in the psalm; it's the crowd's addition.

3. The donkey's answer. Jesus "found a young donkey and sat on it" (12:14), fulfilling Zechariah 9:9. Into the crowd's political hopes Jesus answers with a silent act: he is a king, but a humble one on a donkey's colt, not a conqueror on a warhorse. Zechariah goes on: God says, "I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim," and this king "shall speak peace to the nations" (Zech 9:10).

4. "Fear not." John's quotation reads "Fear not, daughter of Zion," while Zechariah has "Rejoice greatly." "Fear not" may come from Isaiah 40:9 or Zephaniah 3:16, and Zephaniah 3:15 has just said, "The King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst." John combines several texts to stress that this king comes bringing comfort.

5. The disciples understood later. "His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him" (12:16). As in 2:22, some things can only be understood after the cross and resurrection.

Going Deeper: 12:20–28 "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified"

1. The Greeks arrive. "Sir, we wish to see Jesus" (12:21). These Greeks were probably God-fearing Gentiles who had come up to worship at the feast. The Pharisees had just said, "Look, the world has gone after him" (12:19), and immediately representatives of "the world" appear.

2. A grain of wheat. Jesus doesn't directly say whether he will see them. He says, "unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (12:24). The Greeks want to "see" Jesus, but their real meeting with him must wait until after he dies. The cross will open the way for people of every nation to come to him.

3. The same road. "Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life" (12:25). "Hate" is a strong Semitic idiom of contrast, meaning "put second by comparison," not psychological self-loathing. The principle of the grain of wheat applies not only to Jesus but to those who follow him.

4. John's Gethsemane. "Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your name" (12:27–28). John doesn't record the prayer in Gethsemane, but these words carry the same struggle and the same surrender. Jesus is truly human; facing the cross, he is truly troubled. He is also the obedient Son, and he chooses the Father's glory.

5. A voice from heaven. "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again" (12:28). This is the only voice from heaven in John. "Have glorified" refers to Jesus' ministry and signs; "will glorify again" to the coming cross and resurrection.

The point: The parable of the grain of wheat sums up John's whole view of the cross: death isn't defeat but the only way to bear much fruit.
Going Deeper: 12:31–33 "When I am lifted up from the earth"

1. Two "nows." "Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out" (12:31). The cross looks like the world judging Jesus; in fact the world is judged at the cross, and the penalty sinners deserved falls on the one lifted up in our place. "The ruler of this world" is Satan (14:30; 16:11). At the cross, the powers of darkness that seem to win are actually cast out.

2. The third "lifted up." "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself" (12:32). John explains at once: "He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die" (12:33). This is the last and clearest of the three "lifted up" sayings (3:14; 8:28): raised high on the cross, he is at the same moment exalted in glory.

3. "All people." (Some manuscripts read "all things.") With the Greeks just arrived, "all people" most naturally means people of every kind, Gentiles as well as Jews. It echoes 10:16 and 11:52: gathering into one the scattered children of God.

Going Deeper: 12:37–43 "Isaiah saw his glory"

1. The Book of Signs summed up. "Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him" (12:37). At the end of the Book of Signs John explains this heartbreaking fact with two passages from Isaiah: Isaiah 53:1, "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us?" (as John quotes it, 12:38), and Isaiah 6:10, which John renders, "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart" (12:40). John's form makes explicit that God is the one acting in the hardening.

2. "Therefore they could not believe." This sentence (12:39) is heavy. John says two things at once: they "did not believe" (12:37, their own refusal), and they "could not believe" (12:39, God's judgment hardening their hearts). Scripture often sets these side by side: when people reject the light, God gives them over to the darkness. John does not resolve the two: God sovereignly hardens in judgment (cf. 6:44), and people remain fully responsible for rejecting the light. No one who truly wants to come is turned away (6:37).

3. Whose glory did Isaiah see? "Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him" (12:41). In Isaiah 6 the prophet saw "the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up," while the seraphim cried, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts." John says that what Isaiah saw was Jesus' glory. It's one of John's most direct statements of Jesus' deity. Many scholars also note that Isaiah 6:1 describes the Lord as "high and lifted up," and Isaiah 52:13 says the suffering servant "shall be high and lifted up," with closely matching words. John seems to read the two together: the Lord on the throne and the servant lifted up are the same person.

4. Secret believers. "Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it... for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God" (12:42–43). This echoes 5:44. John doesn't simply condemn secret believers, but he names the problem plainly: fear of losing people's approval.

Meditation

Reflect: Jesus himself is the grain of wheat that fell into the earth and died, so that I could become part of the harvest. Mary's perfume was the natural response of someone greatly loved. As I think of what he gave for me, is there something I've been clutching that begins to loosen? When I fear what people think, is it because I haven't yet tasted enough of the glory that comes from God?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第十三章开始了「荣耀之书」。镜头从公开的群众转到楼上的房间，只剩下耶稣和门徒。洗脚（1-20节）：耶稣脱了衣服，拿手巾束腰，洗门徒的脚。预言被卖（21-30节）：耶稣把蘸过的饼递给犹大，犹大出去了，「那时候是夜间了」。新命令（31-35节）：「我怎样爱你们，你们也要怎样相爱。」预言彼得不认主（36-38节）。

从第十三章到第十七章，是约翰福音独有的「楼上讲论」，占了全书将近五分之一。前十二章记载了大约三年的事奉，接下来的五章，只记载了一个晚上。约翰要我们放慢脚步，听耶稣在受难前对属他的人说的最后的话。

深读 13:1「就爱他们到底」

1. 一节总纲。 这一节是整个荣耀之书的标题：「逾越节以前，耶稣知道自己离世归父的时候到了。他既然爱世间属自己的人，就爱他们到底。」逾越节、时候、离世归父、爱，后面八章都在展开这几个词。

2. 「到底」的两层意思。 「到底」的希腊文是 eis telos，可以是「到最后」（时间上，一直爱到生命的尽头），也可以是「到极致」（程度上，爱到最完全的地步）。约翰很可能两层意思都包括在内。这个 telos（终点、完成）在十字架上会再次出现：耶稣最后说「成了」（tetelestai，19:30），是同一个字根。他爱他们到底，而在十字架上，这爱「成了」。

3. 「属自己的人」。 1:11说「他到自己的地方来，自己的人倒不接待他」，那里的「自己的人」指拒绝他的以色列。在这里，「属自己的人」是接待他的门徒。神迹之书以被拒绝开始，荣耀之书以爱属自己的人开始。

深读 13:3-11 脱了衣服，拿手巾束腰

1. 他知道自己是谁。 「耶稣知道父已将万有交在他手里，且知道自己是从神出来的，又要归到神那里去，就离席站起来……」（13:3-4）约翰特意先写耶稣的身份，再写他的举动。洗脚不是因为他忘了自己是谁，而恰恰是因为他知道。真正的谦卑不是自我贬低，而是知道自己是谁、在父爱中稳妥的人，甘心去服事。

2. 奴仆的工作。 在当时，洗客人的脚是奴仆的工作，有些犹太文献甚至认为这工作太卑微，不该要求犹太奴仆去做。门徒中没有一个人主动去做，路加福音记载他们那晚还在争论谁为大（路22:24）。

3. 一个演出来的比喻。 「脱了衣服」的「脱」（tithēsin），正是10:11「好牧人为羊舍命」的「舍」；洗完以后「穿上衣服」的「穿上」（elaben，13:12），正是10:17-18「舍去，好再取回来」的「取」。许多解经家认为：耶稣放下外衣、俯身洗脚、又取回外衣，就是一个演出来的十字架：放下生命、为人洁净、再取回生命。

4. 「你就与我无分了」。 彼得说：「你永不可洗我的脚！」耶稣说：「我若不洗你，你就与我无分了。」（13:8）这句话显出洗脚不只是谦卑的榜样，更指向耶稣为人洁净罪的工作。不接受他的洁净，就与他无分。

5. 洗澡与洗脚。 彼得又转向另一个极端：「不但我的脚，连手和头也要洗。」耶稣说：「凡洗过澡的人，只要把脚一洗，全身就干净了。」（13:9-10）（有些抄本没有「只要把脚一洗」这几个字。）许多解经家这样理解：信主时，人一次全然被洁净（洗澡）；在每天的行走中，仍需要不断地被洁净（洗脚），如约翰一书1:9所说的认罪与赦免。「你们是干净的，然而不都是干净的」，指的是犹大。

深读 13:12-17「你们也当彼此洗脚」

1. 榜样。 「我是你们的主，你们的夫子，尚且洗你们的脚，你们也当彼此洗脚。我给你们作了榜样。」（13:14-15）「榜样」（hypodeigma）是一个可以照着去做的样式。

2. 要照字面实行吗？ 有些教会把洗脚当作一个礼仪来遵守，这在教会历史上也有先例。多数教会则认为，耶稣要的是洗脚所代表的那种服事：甘心做最卑微的事来服事弟兄姊妹。两种做法都可以，但若只守礼仪而没有那份心，就失去了重点。

3. 「若是去行就有福了」。 「你们既知道这事，若是去行就有福了。」（13:17）知道和去做之间有一段距离，福气在去做的那一边；而能去做的力量，来自先让他洗我们。

深读 13:21-30 一点饼与「那时候是夜间了」

1. 耶稣所爱的门徒。 「有一个门徒，是耶稣所爱的，侧身挨近耶稣的怀里。」（13:23）这是「耶稣所爱的那门徒」第一次出现。当时吃饭是侧躺在矮桌旁，用左肘支撑。「怀里」（kolpos）这个字在1:18也出现过：子「在父怀里」。正如子在父怀里，所以能将父表明出来；这位门徒在耶稣怀里，所以能为耶稣作见证（21:24）。

2. 蘸过的饼。 「我蘸一点饼给谁，就是谁。」（13:26）在当时的筵席上，主人亲手把一块蘸过的饼递给某位客人，可能是一种尊荣的表示。耶稣在最后一刻，仍然向犹大伸出了友谊的手。诗篇41:9的预言在这里应验：「同我吃饭的人用脚踢我。」（13:18）

3. 撒但入了他的心。 「他吃了以后，撒但就入了他的心。」（13:27）约翰同时说了两件事：魔鬼把卖耶稣的意思放在犹大心里（13:2），犹大自己是个贼（12:6）。人的罪与撒但的工作交织在一起，而犹大始终要为自己的选择负责。

4. 「那时候是夜间了」。 「犹大受了那点饼，立刻就出去。那时候是夜间了。」（13:30）这是约翰福音里最短、最沉重的一句话之一。它是一个时间记录，也是一个属灵的描写：犹大离开了世界的光（8:12），走进了黑夜。

深读 13:34-35「我怎样爱你们，你们也要怎样相爱」

1. 新在哪里？ 「爱人如己」在利未记19:18就有了，为什么说是「新命令」？新的是标准：「我怎样爱你们，你们也要怎样相爱。」旧的标准是「如己」，新的标准是「如基督」。基督刚刚用洗脚显明了这爱的样式，不久更要在十字架上显明。

2. 时机。 耶稣说这话，是在犹大出去之后、彼得不认主的预言之前。新命令夹在背叛和失败中间，这不是巧合：那要彼此相爱的门徒群体，本身就是一群会失败、需要被饶恕的人。

3. 世人认出门徒的记号。 「你们若有彼此相爱的心，众人因此就认出你们是我的门徒了。」（13:35）耶稣没有说「你们若有正确的教义」或「你们若有大能的神迹」，而是「彼此相爱」。教会内部的爱，本身就是向世界的见证。

要点：新命令的「新」，不在于要我们爱，而在于爱的尺度：像那位脱下外衣、跪下来洗我们脚、又为我们舍命的主那样去爱。
深读 13:36-38「我愿意为你舍命！」

彼得说：「主啊，我为什么现在不能跟你去？我愿意为你舍命！」（13:37）彼得用的，正是好牧人那句「为……舍命」的说法（tēn psychēn ... thēsō，参10:11）。他真心想做好牧人为羊所做的事，但他还不明白：必须先是好牧人为他舍命，他才能为好牧人舍命。耶稣回答：「鸡叫以先，你要三次不认我。」（13:38）这个故事没有在这里结束：在21:15-19，复活的主会三次问彼得「你爱我吗」，并告诉他，将来他真的会为主舍命。

默想

默想： 耶稣「知道自己是谁」，所以能放下外衣去洗脚。我的服事，是出于知道自己已被主爱到底，还是出于想被人看见？有没有一个人，是我需要「洗他的脚」，而我一直不愿意的？彼得想为主舍命，却先要经历失败和被饶恕。我是否也需要先接受主为我所做的，才有力量为他去做？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 13 opens the Book of Glory. The camera moves from the public crowds to an upper room, with only Jesus and his disciples. The foot washing (vv. 1–20): Jesus lays aside his garments, ties a towel around his waist and washes the disciples' feet. The betrayal foretold (vv. 21–30): Jesus hands Judas a piece of dipped bread, Judas goes out, "and it was night." The new commandment (vv. 31–35): "just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another." Peter's denial foretold (vv. 36–38).

Chapters 13–17 are the Upper Room Discourse, found only in John and making up nearly a fifth of the book. The first twelve chapters covered about three years of ministry; the next five cover a single evening. John wants us to slow down and listen to Jesus' last words to his own before his suffering.

Going Deeper: 13:1 "He loved them to the end"

1. A heading for everything that follows. This verse is the title of the whole Book of Glory: "Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end." Passover, hour, departing to the Father, love: the next eight chapters unfold these words.

2. Two senses of "to the end." "To the end" is eis telos, which can mean "to the last" (in time, loving them until his life's end) or "to the uttermost" (in degree, loving them completely). John likely means both. This telos (end, completion) reappears at the cross: Jesus' last word, "It is finished" (tetelestai, 19:30), shares the root. He loved them to the end, and at the cross that love was "finished."

3. "His own." In 1:11, "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him," "his own" meant the Israel that rejected him. Here "his own" are the disciples who received him. The Book of Signs began with rejection; the Book of Glory begins with love for his own.

Going Deeper: 13:3–11 He Laid Aside His Garments and Tied a Towel Around His Waist

1. He knew who he was. "Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper..." (13:3–4). John deliberately describes Jesus' identity before his action. He washes feet not because he forgot who he was, but precisely because he knew. True humility isn't putting yourself down; it's someone who knows who they are, secure in the Father's love, choosing to serve.

2. A slave's job. Washing guests' feet was a slave's task; some Jewish writings even considered it too menial to require of a Jewish slave. None of the disciples volunteered. Luke records that they were still arguing that night about which of them was the greatest (Luke 22:24).

3. An acted parable. "Laid aside" his garments (tithēsin) is the very verb of 10:11, "lays down his life for the sheep." Afterward he "put on" his garments (elaben, 13:12), the verb of 10:17–18, "lay it down that I may take it up again." Many interpreters see here that Jesus laying aside his robe, stooping to wash, then taking it up again is an acted-out cross: laying down his life, cleansing others, taking his life up again.

4. "You have no share with me." Peter says, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answers, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me" (13:8). This shows the foot washing is more than an example of humility; it points to Jesus' work of cleansing from sin. Refuse his cleansing, and you have no part in him.

5. Bathing and foot washing. Peter swings to the other extreme: "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus says, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean" (13:9–10). (Some manuscripts lack "except for his feet.") Many interpreters take it this way: when we first believe, we are cleansed once and completely (the bath); in our daily walk we still need ongoing cleansing (the feet), the confession and forgiveness of 1 John 1:9. "You are clean, but not every one of you" refers to Judas.

Going Deeper: 13:12–17 "You also ought to wash one another's feet"

1. An example. "If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example" (13:14–15). "Example" (hypodeigma) is a pattern to follow.

2. Should it be done literally? Some churches keep foot washing as a rite, with precedent in church history. Most churches understand Jesus to want the kind of service it represents: willingly doing the lowliest tasks for brothers and sisters. Either practice can be right, but keeping the rite without the heart misses the point.

3. "Blessed are you if you do them." "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them" (13:17). There's a distance between knowing and doing, and the blessing lies on the doing side; and the strength to do it comes from first letting him wash us.

Going Deeper: 13:21–30 A Morsel of Bread and "It Was Night"

1. The disciple whom Jesus loved. "One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table close to Jesus" (13:23), literally "in Jesus' bosom." This is the first appearance of "the disciple whom Jesus loved." Diners then reclined at low tables, leaning on the left elbow. "Bosom" (kolpos) also appears in 1:18: the Son is "at the Father's side," literally "in the bosom of the Father." As the Son, close to the Father, makes the Father known, so this disciple, close to Jesus, bears witness to Jesus (21:24).

2. The dipped morsel. "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it" (13:26). At a banquet then, a host handing a guest a dipped morsel himself may have been a mark of honor. To the last moment, Jesus held out the hand of friendship to Judas. Psalm 41:9 is fulfilled: "He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me" (13:18).

3. Satan entered him. "Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him" (13:27). John says two things together: the devil put the betrayal into Judas's heart (13:2), and Judas himself was a thief (12:6). Human sin and Satan's work are intertwined, and Judas remains responsible for his choice.

4. "And it was night." "So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night" (13:30). It's one of the shortest and heaviest sentences in John. It records the time, and it describes a spiritual reality: Judas left the light of the world (8:12) and walked into the night.

Going Deeper: 13:34–35 "Just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another"

1. What's new? "Love your neighbor as yourself" was already in Leviticus 19:18, so why call this a "new commandment"? What's new is the standard: "just as I have loved you." The old standard was "as yourself"; the new standard is "as Christ." And Christ has just shown what that love looks like with the foot washing, and is about to show it with the cross.

2. The timing. Jesus says this after Judas goes out and before he foretells Peter's denial. The new commandment is set between betrayal and failure, and that's no accident: the community called to love one another is a community of people who fail and need forgiveness.

3. The mark the world will recognize. "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another" (13:35). Jesus didn't say "if you have correct doctrine" or "if you do mighty miracles," but "if you have love for one another." Love within the church is itself a witness to the world.

The point: The "new" in the new commandment isn't that we must love but the measure of love: to love like the Lord who laid aside his robe, knelt to wash our feet and laid down his life for us.
Going Deeper: 13:36–38 "I will lay down my life for you"

Peter says, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you" (13:37). Peter uses the good shepherd's own idiom, "lay down one's life for" (tēn psychēn ... thēsō, cf. 10:11). He sincerely wants to do what the good shepherd does for the sheep, but he doesn't yet understand that the good shepherd must first lay down his life for him before he can lay down his life for the shepherd. Jesus answers, "the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times" (13:38). The story doesn't end here: in 21:15–19 the risen Lord will ask Peter three times, "Do you love me?" and tell him that one day he really will lay down his life for him.

Meditation

Reflect: Jesus "knew who he was," so he could lay aside his robe and wash feet. Does my service flow from knowing I am loved to the end, or from wanting to be seen? Is there someone whose "feet I need to wash," and I've been unwilling? Peter wanted to die for the Lord but first had to go through failure and forgiveness. Do I also need first to receive what the Lord has done for me before I have strength to do anything for him?

entries.verse_text: 耶稣说：「我就是道路、真理、生命；若不藉着我，没有人能到父那里去。我留下平安给你们；我将我的平安赐给你们。我所赐的，不像世人所赐的。你们心里不要忧愁，也不要胆怯。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十四章是楼上讲论的第一部分。门徒刚刚听到三个令人不安的消息：耶稣要离开（13:33），其中一个人要出卖他（13:21），彼得要三次不认他（13:38）。耶稣的第一句话就是：「你们心里不要忧愁。」父家里的住处（1-4节）。多马的问题（5-7节）：「我就是道路、真理、生命。」腓力的问题（8-14节）：「人看见了我，就是看见了父。」另一位保惠师（15-26节）：圣灵要来，父与子要与爱主的人同住。平安（27-31节）：「我留下平安给你们。」

这一章有一个特色：门徒不断打断耶稣发问。多马（14:5）、腓力（14:8）、犹大（不是加略人，14:22）。他们的问题都很诚实，也都显出他们还不明白。耶稣没有责备他们发问，而是借着每一个问题，把他们带得更深。

深读 14:1-3「在我父的家里有许多住处」

1. 「信」是命令还是陈述？ 「你们信神，也当信我。」（14:1）希腊文的两个「信」，形式都可以是直述（你们信），也可以是命令（你们要信）。所以可以译作「你们信神，也信我」，也可以译作「要信神，也要信我」。和合本把第一个当直述、第二个当命令。不论哪一种，耶稣都把信他和信神并列，视为同等。

2. 「住处」不是豪宅。 英文钦定本译作「many mansions」，这来自拉丁文 mansiones，原意是「停留的地方」，不是今天说的「豪宅」。希腊文 monai 来自约翰最爱用的动词 menō（住、常在）。耶稣的重点不是房子有多大，而是有地方让我们住下来、与他同在。

3. 同一个字在23节。 monē 这个字在新约里只出现两次，另一次就在14:23：「我们要到他那里去，与他同住。」第2节说的是将来我们去到父家里住；第23节说的是现在父与子来到我们这里住。约翰福音的盼望总是这样：将来的应许，今天就开始了。

4. 「我必再来」。 「我若去为你们预备了地方，就必再来接你们到我那里去，我在哪里，叫你们也在那里。」（14:3）这个「再来」最直接是指他在末日的再来；有些解经家认为也包括复活后的显现和圣灵的降临。天堂最美的地方不是住处本身，而是「我在哪里，叫你们也在那里」。

深读 14:5-7「我就是道路、真理、生命」

1. 多马的诚实。 「主啊，我们不知道你往哪里去，怎么知道那条路呢？」（14:5）多马要一张地图，耶稣给他一个人。

2. 三个词的关系。 「我就是道路、真理、生命；若不藉着我，没有人能到父那里去。」（14:6）这是七个「我是」中的第六个。三个词不是并列的三样东西，许多解经家认为「道路」是重心，「真理」和「生命」说明他为什么是道路：他是道路，因为他就是真理（启示父），他就是生命（赐人永生）。上下文的问题是「那条路」，而后半句说的也是「到父那里去」。他之所以是道路，是因为他自己要经过十字架、担当我们的罪，到父那里去（14:2-4、28），为我们开了路。

3. 排他性的宣告。 「若不藉着我，没有人能到父那里去。」这是新约中最排他的宣告之一。在一个强调多元的时代，在许多华人认为「各宗教都是劝人为善」的处境里，这句话特别刺耳。但这不是傲慢，而是事实陈述：如果耶稣真是从父那里来、要回到父那里去的那一位（13:3），那么他就是唯一认识路、也唯一是路的。使徒行传4:12说出同样的信息：「除他以外，别无拯救。」

4. 认识与看见。 「你们若认识我，也就认识我的父。从今以后，你们认识他，并且已经看见他。」（14:7）这回到序言：「从来没有人看见神，只有在父怀里的独生子将他表明出来。」（1:18）

深读 14:8-14「人看见了我，就是看见了父」

1. 腓力的请求。 「求主将父显给我们看，我们就知足了。」（14:8）这呼应摩西的请求（出33:18「求你显出你的荣耀给我看」）。人心最深处，想要看见神。

2. 「这样长久」。 耶稣的回答带着叹息：「腓力，我与你们同在这样长久，你还不认识我吗？人看见了我，就是看见了父。」（14:9）三年来，腓力天天看着的那张脸，就是神的脸。

3. 不是形态论。 这句话不是说耶稣就是父，好像同一位神换了不同的面具出现。耶稣马上说：「我在父里面，父在我里面。」（14:10）两位彼此内住，不是同一位。教会后来用「互相内住」来描述这种关系：父与子有别，却彼此完全住在对方里面，所以看见子，就是看见父。

4. 「比这更大的事」。 「我所做的事，信我的人也要做，并且要做比这更大的事，因为我往父那里去。」（14:12）门徒怎么可能做比耶稣更大的事？关键在最后一句：「因为我往父那里去。」耶稣复活升天、差下圣灵以后，福音从一个小地方传到全世界，五旬节一天就有三千人信主。「更大」是指范围和救恩历史的阶段，不一定是更惊人的神迹。

5. 「奉我的名」。 「你们奉我的名无论求什么，我必成就，叫父因儿子得荣耀。」（14:13）「奉我的名」不是一句结尾的咒语，而是按着耶稣的身份和心意来求。所以这应许有一个目的：「叫父因儿子得荣耀。」

深读 14:15-26 另一位保惠师

1. 「另外一位」。 「我要求父，父就另外赐给你们一位保惠师。」（14:16）「另外」是 allos，常有「同一类的另一位」的意思（虽然这个区分不是绝对的）。圣灵是与耶稣同类的另一位帮助者。耶稣在门徒身边做的事，圣灵要继续做，而且要「在你们里面」（14:17）。

2. 「保惠师」是什么？ 希腊文 paraklētos 的原意是「被召到身旁的人」，在法庭上是辩护人、代言人。英文译本有「Comforter」「Counselor」「Advocate」「Helper」等不同译法，各抓住一面。中文译经传统（和合本沿用）译作「保惠师」，常被理解为「保护、施恩惠、教导的老师」，把几种意思合在一起。

3. 耶稣是第一位保惠师。 约翰一书2:1说：「若有人犯罪，在父那里我们有一位中保，就是那义者耶稣基督。」这里的「中保」就是 paraklētos。同一个称号也用在耶稣身上：他在世时是门徒身边的帮助者（14:25），升天后在父面前为我们辩护。所以圣灵被称为「另外一位」保惠师，他要住在我们里面，为耶稣作见证。

4. 「我不撇下你们为孤儿」。 「我不撇下你们为孤儿，我必到你们这里来。」（14:18）门徒怕被丢下。这首先可能指复活后的显现（14:19「你们却看见我」），也延续到圣灵的内住。「我们要到他那里去，与他同住」（14:23），父、子、圣灵，都在这一章里应许要与信徒同在。

5. 圣灵的教导。 「他要将一切的事指教你们，并且要叫你们想起我对你们所说的一切话。」（14:26）这首先是对使徒的应许：圣灵会帮助他们想起并明白耶稣的话，这正是新约圣经得以写成的基础。约翰福音本身，就是这个应许的成就之一（参2:22；12:16）。

深读 14:27-31「我留下平安给你们」

1. 临别的赠礼。 「我留下平安给你们；我将我的平安赐给你们。」（14:27）犹太人见面和道别都说「平安」（shalom）。耶稣在离别前说的，不是一句客套话，而是一份遗产。

2. 不像世人所赐的。 「我所赐的，不像世人所赐的。」世人的平安取决于环境：没有冲突、没有危险。耶稣的平安在他即将被出卖、被钉十字架的那个晚上说出，它不取决于环境，而取决于他自己。

3. 「父是比我大的」。 「你们若爱我，因我到父那里去，就必喜乐，因为父是比我大的。」（14:28）这节经文在教会历史上曾被用来否认子的神性。但在约翰福音的整体中（1:1；5:18；10:30；20:28），这不可能是说子在本质上低于父。正统的解释主要有两种：奥古斯丁等人认为，这是就道成肉身、取了奴仆形像的子而说的；另有教父认为，这是指父是子的源头，就位格的次序而言。两种解释都不否认子与父同等是神。

4. 「起来，我们走吧！」 「起来，我们走吧！」（14:31）然而接下来还有三章讲论。有学者认为讲论是在前往客西马尼园的路上继续的（第十五章的葡萄树比喻也许就在经过葡萄园时说的），也有学者有其他看法。不论如何，这句话提醒我们：耶稣是主动地走向十字架的。

默想

默想： 耶稣在自己最艰难的夜晚，还在对门徒说「你们心里不要忧愁」。今天什么事让我心里忧愁？我能不能把它带到这位说「我就是道路、真理、生命」的主面前？像多马和腓力一样，我心里有什么诚实的问题，可以直接问他？天堂最美的不是住处，而是「我在哪里，叫你们也在那里」，我是否以他本身为盼望？耶稣说「我不撇下你们为孤儿」，在我感到孤单的时候，我是否记得圣灵就住在我里面？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 14 is the first part of the Upper Room Discourse. The disciples have just heard three troubling things: Jesus is leaving (13:33), one of them will betray him (13:21), and Peter will deny him three times (13:38). Jesus' first words are, "Let not your hearts be troubled." Rooms in the Father's house (vv. 1–4). Thomas's question (vv. 5–7): "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." Philip's question (vv. 8–14): "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." Another Helper (vv. 15–26): the Spirit will come, and the Father and the Son will make their home with those who love Jesus. Peace (vv. 27–31): "Peace I leave with you."

One feature of this chapter is that the disciples keep interrupting Jesus with questions: Thomas (14:5), Philip (14:8), Judas (not Iscariot, 14:22). Their questions are honest, and they show the disciples still don't understand. Jesus doesn't rebuke them for asking; he uses each question to take them deeper.

Going Deeper: 14:1–3 "In my Father's house are many rooms"

1. Is "believe" a command or a statement? "Believe in God; believe also in me" (14:1). Both Greek verbs can be read as statements ("you believe") or commands ("believe!"). So it can mean "You believe in God; believe also in me," or "Believe in God; believe also in me." The Chinese Union Version takes the first as a statement and the second as a command. Either way, Jesus places faith in himself on the same level as faith in God.

2. "Rooms," not mansions. The King James has "many mansions," from the Latin mansiones, which meant "places to stay," not grand houses. The Greek monai comes from John's favorite verb, menō (to remain, abide). Jesus' point isn't the size of the house but that there is a place for us to settle and be with him.

3. The same word in verse 23. Monē appears only twice in the New Testament, the other time in 14:23: "we will come to him and make our home with him." Verse 2 speaks of our going to dwell in the Father's house in the future; verse 23 speaks of the Father and the Son coming to dwell with us now. John's hope is always like this: the future promise begins today.

4. "I will come again." "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also" (14:3). This "coming again" most directly refers to his return at the end; some interpreters think it also includes the resurrection appearances and the coming of the Spirit. The best thing about heaven isn't the room itself but "where I am you may be also."

Going Deeper: 14:5–7 "I am the way, and the truth, and the life"

1. Thomas's honesty. "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" (14:5). Thomas wants a map; Jesus gives him a person.

2. How the three words relate. "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (14:6). This is the sixth of the seven "I am" sayings. The three words aren't three separate things. Many interpreters see "the way" as the main point, with "the truth" and "the life" explaining why he is the way: he is the way because he is the truth (revealing the Father) and the life (giving eternal life). The question in context is about "the way," and the second half of the verse is about "coming to the Father." He is the way because he himself goes to the Father through the cross, bearing our sin (14:2–4, 28), opening the way for us.

3. An exclusive claim. "No one comes to the Father except through me." This is one of the most exclusive claims in the New Testament, and it grates in an age that prizes pluralism. But it isn't arrogance; it's a statement of fact. If Jesus truly came from the Father and is returning to the Father (13:3), then he alone knows the way and he alone is the way. Acts 4:12 says the same: "there is salvation in no one else."

4. Knowing and seeing. "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him" (14:7). This returns to the Prologue: "No one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known" (1:18).

Going Deeper: 14:8–14 "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father"

1. Philip's request. "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us" (14:8). This echoes Moses' request (Ex 33:18, "Please show me your glory"). The deepest longing of the human heart is to see God.

2. "So long." Jesus' answer carries a sigh: "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (14:9). For three years the face Philip looked at every day was the face of God.

3. Not modalism. This doesn't mean Jesus is the Father, as if one God appeared wearing different masks. Jesus immediately says, "I am in the Father and the Father is in me" (14:10). Two persons dwelling in each other, not one and the same. The church later described this as mutual indwelling: Father and Son are distinct yet fully dwell in each other, so to see the Son is to see the Father.

4. "Greater works than these." "Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father" (14:12). How could disciples do greater works than Jesus? The key is the last clause: "because I am going to the Father." After Jesus rose, ascended and sent the Spirit, the gospel spread from one small land to the whole world; on the day of Pentecost alone, three thousand believed. "Greater" refers to scope and to the stage of salvation history, not necessarily to more spectacular miracles.

5. "In my name." "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son" (14:13). "In my name" isn't a closing formula but asking in keeping with who Jesus is and what he wants. So the promise has a purpose: "that the Father may be glorified in the Son."

Going Deeper: 14:15–26 Another Helper

1. "Another." "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper" (14:16). "Another" is allos, which often means "another of the same kind" (though the distinction isn't absolute). The Spirit is the same kind of helper as Jesus. What Jesus did beside the disciples, the Spirit will continue to do, and he will be "in you" (14:17).

2. What is a "Helper"? The Greek paraklētos originally means "one called alongside," in a courtroom an advocate or counsel for the defense. English versions have "Comforter," "Counselor," "Advocate," "Helper," each catching one side of it. The Chinese translation tradition, followed by the Chinese Union Version, uses baohuishi, often explained as "a teacher who protects and shows kindness," combining several of these senses.

3. Jesus is the first Helper. First John 2:1 says, "if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." "Advocate" there is paraklētos. The same title is used of Jesus: he was the disciples' helper while he was with them (14:25), and now pleads our case before the Father. So the Spirit is called "another" Helper, who will live in us and bear witness to Jesus.

4. "I will not leave you as orphans." "I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you" (14:18). The disciples were afraid of being left behind. This most likely refers first to his resurrection appearances (14:19, "you will see me"), and continues in the Spirit's indwelling. "We will come to him and make our home with him" (14:23): Father, Son and Spirit all promise in this chapter to be with believers.

5. The Spirit's teaching. "He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you" (14:26). This is first a promise to the apostles: the Spirit would help them remember and understand Jesus' words, which is the foundation on which the New Testament was written. John's Gospel itself is one fulfillment of this promise (cf. 2:22; 12:16).

Going Deeper: 14:27–31 "Peace I leave with you"

1. A parting gift. "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you" (14:27). Jews greeted and parted with "peace" (shalom). What Jesus says before leaving isn't a pleasantry but a bequest.

2. "Not as the world gives." "Not as the world gives do I give to you." The world's peace depends on circumstances: no conflict, no danger. Jesus speaks of his peace on the night he will be betrayed and the eve of his crucifixion. It doesn't depend on circumstances; it depends on him.

3. "The Father is greater than I." "If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I" (14:28). In church history this verse has been used to deny the Son's deity. But within John as a whole (1:1; 5:18; 10:30; 20:28), it can't mean the Son is lesser in essence. Orthodox interpretation has taken two main lines. Augustine and others read it of the incarnate Son, who took the form of a servant. Other fathers read it of the Father as the source of the Son, in the order of the persons. Neither reading denies that the Son is equally God with the Father.

4. "Rise, let us go from here." "Rise, let us go from here" (14:31). Yet three more chapters of discourse follow. Some scholars think the discourse continued on the way to Gethsemane (perhaps the vine of chapter 15 was spoken passing a vineyard); others take different views. Either way, the words remind us that Jesus walked toward the cross of his own accord.

Meditation

Reflect: On the hardest night of his life, Jesus was still telling his disciples, "Let not your hearts be troubled." What is troubling my heart today? Can I bring it to the Lord who says, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life"? Like Thomas and Philip, what honest question do I have that I could ask him directly? Heaven's best is not the room but "where I am you may be also." Is he himself my hope? Jesus said, "I will not leave you as orphans." When I feel alone, do I remember that the Spirit lives in me?

entries.title_en: I Am the True Vine: Abide in Me

人为朋友舍命，人的爱心没有比这个大的。

entries.verse_text: 我是葡萄树，你们是枝子。常在我里面的，我也常在他里面，这人就多结果子；因为离了我，你们就不能做什么。人为朋友舍命，人的爱心没有比这个大的。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十五章是楼上讲论的第二部分。葡萄树与枝子（1-11节）：「我是真葡萄树……你们要常在我里面。」朋友与彼此相爱（12-17节）：「人为朋友舍命，人的爱心没有比这个大的。」世界的恨恶（18-25节）：「世人若恨你们，你们知道，恨你们以先已经恨我了。」圣灵与门徒的见证（26-27节）。

前十一节里，「常在」（menō，也译「住」）这个字出现了十次以上。如果要用一个词总结这一章，就是「常在」：常在他里面、常在他的话里、常在他的爱里。这个字在约翰福音一开始就出现了：施洗约翰看见圣灵降下来「住在」耶稣身上（1:32），最初的门徒问「拉比，在哪里住？」又「与他同住」（1:38-39）。到了第十五章，这份「同住」从地方上的同住，变成了生命上的联合。

深读 15:1-3「我是真葡萄树」

1. 以色列是葡萄树。 在旧约里，葡萄树常是以色列的象征：「你从埃及挪出一棵葡萄树，赶出外邦人，把这树栽上。」（诗80:8）但这棵葡萄树一再令神失望：「他指望的是公平，谁知倒有暴虐。」（赛5:7）「我栽你是上等的葡萄树……你怎么向我变为外邦葡萄树的坏枝子呢？」（耶2:21）

2. 「真」葡萄树。 所以当耶稣说「我是真葡萄树」，他是在说：以色列应该是、却没有成为的那棵树，就是我。他是那位真以色列，结出神一直期待的果子。这是七个「我是」中的最后一个。神的子民不再按血统来划分，而在于是否与他相连：枝子属于葡萄树。

3. 剪去与修理。 「凡属我不结果子的枝子，他就剪去；凡结果子的，他就修理干净，使枝子结果子更多。」（15:2）有一个流行的说法，认为「剪去」（airei）应该译作「举起来」，像园丁把垂在地上的枝子扶起来。这个字确实可以有「举起」的意思，但在这里的上下文（15:6「丢在外面……烧了」）中，多数解经家和译本都理解为「除去」。

4. 一语双关。 「修理干净」（kathairei）和下一节的「干净」（katharoi）是同一个字根。「现在你们因我讲给你们的道，已经干净了。」（15:3）门徒已经被修剪过，用的工具是耶稣的话。神修剪我们，很多时候是透过他的话：它指出我们需要放下的，也洁净我们。

深读 15:4-8「离了我，你们就不能做什么」

1. 常在是彼此的。 「你们要常在我里面，我也常在你们里面。」（15:4）这不是单方面的努力，而是一种关系：枝子留在树上，树的生命就流进枝子里。

2. 「不能做什么」。 「我是葡萄树，你们是枝子。常在我里面的，我也常在他里面，这人就多结果子；因为离了我，你们就不能做什么。」（15:5）不是「能做的比较少」，而是「不能做什么」。人可以很忙、很有成就，却在神眼中没有结出一个属灵的果子。

3. 果子是什么？ 上下文给了线索：遵守他的命令（15:10）、喜乐（15:11）、彼此相爱（15:12）、为他作见证（15:27），以及因此有人信主（15:16，「分派你们去结果子」）。果子是基督的生命在我们身上自然的流露，加拉太书5:22称之为「圣灵所结的果子」。

4. 丢在外面的枝子。 「人若不常在我里面，就像枝子丢在外面枯干，人拾起来，扔在火里烧了。」（15:6）这是一个严肃的警告。这是否表示真信徒会失去救恩？福音派内部有不同的理解。改革宗传统认为，这些枝子是表面上与基督有关联、却从未真正与他联合的人，像犹大（他刚刚离开这个房间，13:30）；约翰一书2:19也说「他们从我们中间出去，却不是属我们的」。（改革宗也认为这些警告是真实的，正是神用来保守信徒坚忍到底的方法之一。）另一些传统则认为真信徒确有失落的危险。各方都同意：这节经文的目的不是让人猜测别人的结局，而是呼召每一个人常在他里面。

5. 祷告与果子。 「你们若常在我里面，我的话也常在你们里面，凡你们所愿意的，祈求，就给你们成就。」（15:7）条件是「我的话也常在你们里面」：一个被他的话塑造的人，所求的会越来越是主所要的。

深读 15:12-17「乃称你们为朋友」

1. 最大的爱。 「人为朋友舍命，人的爱心没有比这个大的。」（15:13）耶稣说这话的时候，离他舍命只有几个小时。这不是一句抽象的道德格言，而是他即将要做的事。罗马书5:8、10更进一步：「惟有基督在我们还作罪人的时候为我们死」，并且是「我们作仇敌的时候」。他为这些「朋友」舍命，代替他们担当罪孽；而他们原本是他的仇敌。

2. 从仆人到朋友。 「以后我不再称你们为仆人，因仆人不知道主人所做的事。我乃称你们为朋友。」（15:15）在旧约里，被称为神的「朋友」的是亚伯拉罕（赛41:8；代下20:7；雅2:23）；摩西则是神与他说话「好像人与朋友说话一般」（出33:11）。现在这个称号临到门徒。朋友与仆人的区别，不在于是否顺服（15:14「你们若遵行我所吩咐的，就是我的朋友了」），而在于是否被告知主人的心意。

3. 「是我拣选了你们」。 「不是你们拣选了我，是我拣选了你们，并且分派你们去结果子，叫你们的果子常存。」（15:16）当时的拉比通常是由门徒选择老师；耶稣却主动拣选门徒。这份拣选不是为了特权，而是为了差遣：「分派你们去结果子」。

要点：枝子不需要用力「挤出」果子，它只需要留在树上。常在基督里，不是一种技巧，而是一份关系：留在他的话里、他的爱里，果子自然会结出来。
深读 15:18-27 世界的恨恶与两种见证

1. 被恨是正常的。 「世人若恨你们，你们知道，恨你们以先已经恨我了。」（15:18）门徒不必惊讶。「你们若属世界，世界必爱属自己的；只因你们不属世界……所以世界就恨你们。」（15:19）「世界」在这里又是那个与神为敌的人类社会（参3:16的讨论）。

2. 「无故地恨我」。 「这要应验他们律法上所写的话，说：『他们无故地恨我。』」（15:25）这句话出自诗篇（35:19；69:4）。耶稣称诗篇为「律法」，这在当时是常见的用法：「律法」可以泛指整本旧约。诗篇69篇在约翰福音里已经出现过（2:17），它是受苦义人的诗篇。

3. 圣灵的见证与门徒的见证。 「我要从父那里差保惠师来，就是从父出来真理的圣灵；他来了，就要为我作见证。你们也要作见证。」（15:26-27）在一个恨恶的世界里，门徒不是孤军作战：圣灵与他们一同作见证。「从父出来」这句话后来成为尼西亚－君士坦丁堡信经（381年）的用语。东西方教会关于「和子」的争论也引用这节；但要注意，这里是耶稣亲自「从父那里差」圣灵，许多解经家认为本节首先讲圣灵的差遣，而不是圣灵在永恒中从父「发出」。

默想

默想： 「离了我，你们就不能做什么。」耶稣说「现在你们……已经干净了」，又说「是我拣选了你们」。在这份已经成就的关系里，我最近的忙碌中，有多少是从常在他里面流出来的？神现在是否正在用他的话「修剪」我生命中的某一部分？耶稣称我为「朋友」，这个称呼怎样改变我对祷告、对顺服的看法？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 15 is the second part of the Upper Room Discourse. The vine and the branches (vv. 1–11): "I am the true vine... Abide in me." Friends who love one another (vv. 12–17): "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lays down his life for his friends." The world's hatred (vv. 18–25): "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you." The witness of the Spirit and the disciples (vv. 26–27).

In the first eleven verses the word "abide" (menō, also "remain," "dwell") appears ten times or more. If one word sums up this chapter, it's "abide": abide in him, in his word, in his love. The word appears at the very start of John: John the Baptist sees the Spirit descend and "remain" on Jesus (1:32), and the first disciples ask, "Rabbi, where are you staying?" and "stayed with him" (1:38–39). Chapter 15 turns that staying from a matter of location into a matter of life.

Going Deeper: 15:1–3 "I am the true vine"

1. Israel as the vine. In the Old Testament the vine is often a symbol of Israel: "You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it" (Ps 80:8). But this vine repeatedly disappointed God: "he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed" (Isa 5:7); "I planted you a choice vine, wholly of pure seed. How then have you turned degenerate and become a wild vine?" (Jer 2:21).

2. The "true" vine. So when Jesus says, "I am the true vine," he's saying: the tree Israel was meant to be but never became, that is me. He is the true Israel, bearing the fruit God always looked for. This is the last of the seven "I am" sayings. God's people are no longer defined by ethnicity but by union with him: the branches belong to the vine.

3. Taking away and pruning. "Every branch of mine that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit" (15:2). A popular idea holds that "takes away" (airei) should be translated "lifts up," like a gardener raising branches off the ground. The word can mean "lift," but in this context (15:6, "thrown away... burned") most interpreters and translations take it as "remove."

4. A play on words. "Prunes" (kathairei) and "clean" (katharoi) in the next verse share a root. "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you" (15:3). The disciples have already been pruned, and the tool was Jesus' word. God often prunes us through his word: it shows us what we need to let go of, and it cleanses us.

Going Deeper: 15:4–8 "Apart from me you can do nothing"

1. Abiding is mutual. "Abide in me, and I in you" (15:4). This isn't one-sided effort but a relationship: the branch stays on the vine, and the vine's life flows into the branch.

2. "Nothing." "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing" (15:5). Not "less," but "nothing." A person can be very busy and very successful and yet, in God's eyes, bear no spiritual fruit at all.

3. What is the fruit? The context gives clues: keeping his commandments (15:10), joy (15:11), loving one another (15:12), bearing witness to him (15:27), and people coming to faith as a result (15:16, "appointed you that you should go and bear fruit"). Fruit is the natural overflow of Christ's life in us, what Galatians 5:22 calls "the fruit of the Spirit."

4. Branches thrown away. "If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned" (15:6). This is a solemn warning. Does it mean true believers can lose their salvation? Evangelicals understand it differently. The Reformed tradition holds that these branches are people outwardly connected to Christ who were never truly united to him, like Judas (who had just left this room, 13:30); 1 John 2:19 says, "They went out from us, but they were not of us." (Reformed theology also holds that these warnings are real, one of the means God uses to keep believers persevering.) Other traditions hold that true believers can in fact fall away. All agree that the verse isn't meant to make us speculate about other people's end but to call each of us to abide in him.

5. Prayer and fruit. "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you" (15:7). The condition is "my words abide in you": a person shaped by his words will increasingly ask for what Christ wills.

Going Deeper: 15:12–17 "I have called you friends"

1. The greatest love. "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lays down his life for his friends" (15:13). When Jesus said this, he was only hours from laying down his life. It isn't an abstract moral maxim; it's what he was about to do. Romans 5:8 and 10 go further: "while we were still sinners, Christ died for us," and "while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son." The "friends" he died for, in their place and bearing their sin, were once his enemies.

2. From servants to friends. "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends" (15:15). In the Old Testament Abraham is called God's "friend" (Isa 41:8; 2 Chr 20:7; Jas 2:23), and of Moses it is said the LORD spoke with him "as a man speaks to his friend" (Ex 33:11). Now the title is given to the disciples. The difference between friend and servant isn't whether they obey (15:14, "You are my friends if you do what I command you") but whether they are told the master's mind.

3. "I chose you." "You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide" (15:16). In those days disciples usually chose their rabbi; Jesus chose his disciples. That choice was not for privilege but for mission: "appointed you that you should go and bear fruit."

The point: A branch doesn't strain to squeeze out fruit; it only needs to stay on the vine. Abiding in Christ isn't a technique but a relationship: staying in his word and his love, and the fruit comes.
Going Deeper: 15:18–27 The World's Hatred and Two Witnesses

1. Being hated is normal. "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (15:18). The disciples needn't be surprised. "If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world... therefore the world hates you" (15:19). "The world" here is again human society set against God (see the discussion of 3:16).

2. "Hated me without a cause." "But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause'" (15:25). The words come from the Psalms (35:19; 69:4). Jesus calls the Psalms "Law," a common usage then for the whole Old Testament. Psalm 69 has already appeared in John (2:17); it's a psalm of the suffering righteous one.

3. The Spirit's witness and the disciples' witness. "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness" (15:26–27). In a hostile world the disciples don't fight alone: the Spirit bears witness alongside them. "Who proceeds from the Father" later became the language of the Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381). This verse also figures in the later East–West dispute over "and from the Son" (filioque); note that here Jesus himself sends the Spirit "from the Father," and many interpreters think the verse speaks first of the Spirit's mission rather than his eternal origin.

Meditation

Reflect: "Apart from me you can do nothing." Jesus says, "Already you are clean," and "I chose you." Within that settled relationship, how much of my recent busyness has flowed from abiding in him? Is God using his word right now to "prune" some part of my life? Jesus calls me his "friend." How does that change the way I think about prayer and obedience?

entries.title_en: Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World

verse_parts.text: 只等真理的圣灵来了，他要引导你们明白一切的真理；因为他不是凭自己说的，乃是把他所听见的都说出来，并要把将来的事告诉你们。
我将这些事告诉你们，是要叫你们在我里面有平安。在世上，你们有苦难；但你们可以放心，我已经胜了世界。」

entries.verse_text: 只等真理的圣灵来了，他要引导你们明白一切的真理；因为他不是凭自己说的，乃是把他所听见的都说出来，并要把将来的事告诉你们。我将这些事告诉你们，是要叫你们在我里面有平安。在世上，你们有苦难；但你们可以放心，我已经胜了世界。」
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十六章是楼上讲论的第三部分，也是讲论的结尾。将来的逼迫（1-4节）：「凡杀你们的就以为是事奉神。」圣灵的工作（5-15节）：「我去是与你们有益的。」圣灵要为罪、为义、为审判使世界知罪，又要引导门徒明白一切的真理。忧愁变为喜乐（16-24节）：「等不多时，你们就不得见我；再等不多时，你们还要见我。」我已经胜了世界（25-33节）。

门徒在这一章里最大的困惑是「不多的时候」（16:16-18）：他们反复问这句话是什么意思。耶稣说的是他的死与复活：三天之内，他们会从最深的忧愁走到最大的喜乐。但这个模式也是整个基督徒生命的模式：在等待主再来的「不多的时候」里，我们经历忧愁，却确知它要变为喜乐。

深读 16:7「我去是与你们有益的」

1. 难以置信的一句话。 「然而，我将真情告诉你们，我去是与你们有益的；我若不去，保惠师就不到你们这里来；我若去，就差他来。」（16:7）门徒最不想听到的就是耶稣要离开，耶稣却说这对他们有益。

2. 为什么？ 耶稣在世的时候，一次只能在一个地方，和少数人在一起。圣灵来了以后，就住在每一个信徒里面（14:17），在世界的每一个角落。而且，如7:39所说，新约时代圣灵的浇灌，要等到耶稣得荣耀之后。十字架、复活、升天，是圣灵降临的前提。

3. 今天的我们。 这也是对今天读者的安慰。我们常想：如果我能像门徒那样亲眼看见耶稣就好了。耶稣说：有圣灵住在你里面，比那更好，因为借着圣灵，基督自己与我们同在（14:18、23），而20:29也说「没有看见就信的有福了」。

深读 16:8-11 为罪、为义、为审判

1. 和合本的「自己责备自己」。 和合本译作「他既来了，就要叫世人为罪、为义、为审判，自己责备自己」。希腊文的结构是「他要使世界知罪」（elenxei），主词是圣灵。这个动词 elenchō 的意思是「揭露、证明有罪、使人知罪」，像法庭上检察官揭露罪证。和合本的「自己责备自己」点出了结果（人的良心被定罪），而原文强调的是圣灵主动的工作。

2. 三件事的解释。 耶稣自己解释了三件事（16:9-11），但这几节很简洁，解经家有不同的理解。一个常见的读法是： - 为罪，「是因他们不信我」：圣灵要揭露世界最根本的罪：不信耶稣。 - 为义，「是因我往父那里去」：世界判定耶稣是罪人，把他钉在十字架上；但父接纳他回到自己那里，证明他才是义的。圣灵要揭露世界对「义」的错误判断。（也有解经家认为，三项都是在揭露世界自己的罪、自己虚假的义和错误的审判。） - 为审判，「是因这世界的王受了审判」：十字架看起来是世界审判了耶稣，实际上是撒但被审判了（12:31）。

3. 圣灵在传福音中的角色。 这段经文告诉我们，让人认罪悔改，不是传道人的口才能做到的，而是圣灵的工作。门徒的任务是作见证（15:27），圣灵的任务是使人知罪。

深读 16:12-15「他要引导你们明白一切的真理」

1. 「你们现在担当不了」。 「我还有好些事要告诉你们，但你们现在担当不了。」（16:12）有些真理，要等到十字架和复活之后才能明白。

2. 引导进入真理。 「只等真理的圣灵来了，他要引导你们明白一切的真理；因为他不是凭自己说的，乃是把他所听见的都说出来，并要把将来的事告诉你们。」（16:13）这首先是对使徒的应许，和14:26一样。圣灵引导使徒明白并记录关于基督的真理，这正是新约圣经得以写成的基础。这节经文不是说每一个信徒都会直接领受新的启示，而是说圣灵借着使徒所传的话，引导教会进入真理。

3. 圣灵荣耀基督。 「他要荣耀我，因为他要将受于我的告诉你们。」（16:14）圣灵的工作不是把注意力引向自己，而是引向基督。要辨别某种所谓「属灵」的经验或教导，最好的试金石就是：它是否荣耀基督？

4. 三位一体的交流。 「凡父所有的，都是我的，所以我说，他要将受于我的告诉你们。」（16:15）父所有的属于子，子所有的由圣灵传达给门徒。在这短短一节里，可以看到父、子、圣灵之间完美的交流。

深读 16:20-24 生产的妇人

1. 一个熟悉的比喻。 「妇人生产的时候就忧愁，因为她的时候到了；既生了孩子，就不再记念那苦楚，因为欢喜世上生了一个人。」（16:21）旧约常用生产的痛苦来描写神子民在新时代来临前的苦难（赛26:17-18；弥4:9-10）；而16:22「我要再见你们，你们的心就喜乐了」，也与以赛亚书66:14相呼应。

2. 「她的时候」。 「因为她的时候到了」，用的是 hōra，正是整卷书里耶稣的「时候」的那个字。门徒的忧愁和耶稣的十字架，是同一个「时候」：痛苦是真实的，但它是生产的痛苦，不是毫无意义的痛苦。

3. 不是取代，而是转变。 「你们的忧愁要变为喜乐。」（16:20）不是忧愁之后来了另一样东西，而是忧愁本身被转变：生产的痛苦本身变成了新生命的喜乐。十字架本身，变成了救恩。

4. 没有人能夺去的喜乐。 「我要再见你们，你们的心就喜乐了；这喜乐也没有人能夺去。」（16:22）建立在复活上的喜乐，没有任何环境能夺走。

5. 两种「问」。 「到那日，你们什么也就不问我了……你们若向父求什么，他必因我的名赐给你们。」（16:23）这节有两个不同的动词：「问」（erōtaō）和「求」（aiteō）。erōtaō 本身也可指请求（如16:26；17:9），但按16:19的上下文，这里多半指发问。和合本很好地分辨了出来。门徒现在充满了问题（16:17-19）；复活以后，他们的问题会得到解答，而他们可以直接奉耶稣的名向父祈求。

深读 16:32-33「我已经胜了世界」

1. 被撇下，却不孤单。 「看哪，时候将到，且是已经到了，你们要分散，各归自己的地方去，留下我独自一人；其实我不是独自一人，因为有父与我同在。」（16:32）耶稣知道门徒会在几个小时内离开他。他没有责备，只是说：父与我同在。

2. 在他里面有平安，在世上有苦难。 「我将这些事告诉你们，是要叫你们在我里面有平安。在世上，你们有苦难。」（16:33）两个地点、两种处境，同时成立：在世上，门徒有苦难；在基督里，他们有平安。基督徒的平安不是没有苦难，而是在苦难中，有基督作我们更深的安息之所。

3. 「我已经胜了世界」。 「但你们可以放心，我已经胜了世界。」「胜了」（nenikēka）是完成时，表示一个已经完成、并持续有效的胜利。耶稣说这话的时候，还没有被捉拿，还没有上十字架；但他说得好像已经完成了。在他眼中，十字架不是可能的失败，而是确定的胜利。约翰一书5:4接着说：「使我们胜了世界的，就是我们的信心。」

要点：讲论以「我已经胜了世界」作结。门徒即将四散，耶稣即将被钉，但他宣告的不是「我会尽力」，而是「我已经胜了」。
默想

默想： 耶稣说「我去是与你们有益的」，我是否真的相信，借着住在我里面的圣灵，基督自己就与我同在？我现在的忧愁，在神手中不是白白的痛苦；而最终使它变为喜乐的，是「我要再见你们」：是见到他自己。「在世上，你们有苦难；但你们可以放心，我已经胜了世界。」今天我需要把哪一样苦难，放在这个已经完成的胜利之下？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 16 is the third part of the Upper Room Discourse and its conclusion. Persecution to come (vv. 1–4): "whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God." The Spirit's work (vv. 5–15): "it is to your advantage that I go away." The Spirit will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment, and will guide the disciples into all the truth. Sorrow turned to joy (vv. 16–24): "A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me." I have overcome the world (vv. 25–33).

The disciples' biggest puzzle in this chapter is "a little while" (16:16–18); they keep asking what it means. Jesus is speaking of his death and resurrection: within three days they will move from the deepest sorrow to the greatest joy. But the pattern also shapes the whole Christian life. In the "little while" of waiting for the Lord's return, we know sorrow, yet we know for certain that it will turn to joy.

Going Deeper: 16:7 "It is to your advantage that I go away"

1. A hard saying to believe. "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you" (16:7). The last thing the disciples wanted to hear was that Jesus was leaving, and he says it's for their good.

2. Why? On earth Jesus could be in only one place at a time, with a few people. When the Spirit comes, he dwells in every believer (14:17), in every corner of the world. And as 7:39 says, the new-covenant outpouring of the Spirit had to wait until Jesus was glorified. The cross, resurrection and ascension are the precondition of the Spirit's coming.

3. For us today. This comforts today's readers too. We often think, if only I could have seen Jesus with my own eyes like the disciples. Jesus says that having the Spirit live in you is better than that, because through the Spirit Christ himself is with us (14:18, 23), and 20:29 blesses "those who have not seen and yet have believed."

Going Deeper: 16:8–11 Concerning Sin, Righteousness and Judgment

1. The Chinese Union Version's "reproach itself." The Chinese Union Version renders this "he will make the world, concerning sin, righteousness and judgment, reproach itself." The Greek structure is "he will convict the world" (elenxei), with the Spirit as subject. The verb elenchō means to expose, to prove guilty, to convict, like a prosecutor laying out the evidence. The Chinese rendering highlights the result (the conscience condemned), while the Greek stresses the Spirit's active work.

2. The three items explained. Jesus explains the three items himself (16:9–11), but very briefly, and interpreters differ. One common reading: - Concerning sin, "because they do not believe in me": the Spirit exposes that the world's most basic sin is not believing in Jesus. - Concerning righteousness, "because I go to the Father": the world judged Jesus a sinner and crucified him, but the Father received him back to himself, proving that he is the righteous one. The Spirit exposes the world's false verdict about righteousness. (Other interpreters read all three items as exposing the world's own sin, its false righteousness and its false judgment.) - Concerning judgment, "because the ruler of this world is judged": the cross looks like the world judging Jesus, but in fact Satan is judged (12:31).

3. The Spirit's role in evangelism. This passage tells us that bringing people to conviction and repentance isn't something a preacher's eloquence can do; it's the Spirit's work. The disciples' task is to bear witness (15:27); the Spirit's task is to convict.

Going Deeper: 16:12–15 "He will guide you into all the truth"

1. "You cannot bear them now." "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now" (16:12). Some truths could only be understood after the cross and resurrection.

2. Guided into the truth. "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come" (16:13). As in 14:26, this is first a promise to the apostles. The Spirit guided them to understand and record the truth about Christ, which is the foundation on which the New Testament was written. The verse doesn't say every believer will receive new revelation directly; it says the Spirit guides the church into the truth through the apostles' word.

3. The Spirit glorifies Christ. "He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you" (16:14). The Spirit's work doesn't draw attention to himself but to Christ. A good test of any supposedly "spiritual" experience or teaching is whether it glorifies Christ.

4. Communion within the Trinity. "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you" (16:15). What the Father has belongs to the Son, and what the Son has the Spirit makes known to the disciples. In this one short verse we glimpse perfect communion among Father, Son and Spirit.

Going Deeper: 16:20–24 A Woman in Labor

1. A familiar image. "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world" (16:21). The Old Testament often uses the pain of childbirth for the sufferings of God's people before the new age comes (Isa 26:17–18; Mic 4:9–10), and 16:22, "I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice," closely echoes Isaiah 66:14.

2. "Her hour." "Because her hour has come" uses hōra, the very word for Jesus' "hour" throughout the book. The disciples' sorrow and Jesus' cross belong to the same "hour": the pain is real, but it's the pain of birth, not meaningless pain.

3. Not replaced but transformed. "Your sorrow will turn into joy" (16:20). It isn't that something else comes after the sorrow; the sorrow itself is transformed, as labor pain becomes the joy of new life. The cross itself becomes salvation.

4. Joy no one can take away. "I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you" (16:22). Joy founded on the resurrection can't be taken away by any circumstance.

5. Two kinds of "asking." "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you" (16:23). The verse uses two different verbs, erōtaō and aiteō. Erōtaō can mean either "question" or "request" (cf. 16:26; 17:9), but in light of 16:19 it most likely means "ask questions" here, while aiteō means "make requests." The Chinese Union Version distinguishes them well. The disciples are full of questions now (16:17–19). After the resurrection their questions will be answered, and they can make requests directly to the Father in Jesus' name.

Going Deeper: 16:32–33 "I have overcome the world"

1. Left alone. "Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me" (16:32). Jesus knows the disciples will leave him within hours. He doesn't rebuke them; he simply says, the Father is with me.

2. Peace in him, tribulation in the world. "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation" (16:33). Two places, two conditions, both true at once: in the world the disciples will have tribulation; in Christ they have peace. Christian peace isn't the absence of trouble but having Christ as a deeper refuge within it.

3. "I have overcome the world." "But take heart; I have overcome the world." "Have overcome" (nenikēka) is perfect tense: a victory completed and still in force. When Jesus says this, he hasn't yet been arrested or crucified, but he speaks as though it's already done. In his eyes the cross isn't a possible defeat but a certain victory. First John 5:4 continues: "this is the victory that has overcome the world, our faith."

The point: The discourse ends with "I have overcome the world." The disciples are about to scatter and Jesus is about to be crucified, but what he declares isn't "I'll do my best" but "I have overcome."
Meditation

Reflect: Jesus said, "it is to your advantage that I go away." Do I truly believe that through the Spirit who lives in me, Christ himself is with me? My present sorrow is not wasted pain in God's hands; what finally turns it to joy is "I will see you again": seeing him. "In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world." What trouble do I need to place under that finished victory today?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第十七章是新约中记载耶稣最长的一篇祷告。楼上讲论结束了，耶稣「举目望天」，门徒在旁边听着他与父说话。十六世纪的路德宗神学家（一般认为是基特雷乌斯）称它为「大祭司的祷告」，因为耶稣在这里像大祭司一样，在献上自己之前为百姓代求。为自己祷告（1-5节）：「愿你荣耀你的儿子。」为门徒祷告（6-19节）：「求你保守他们……用真理使他们成圣。」为将来的信徒祷告（20-26节）：「使他们都合而为一。」

这篇祷告从耶稣自己，向外一圈圈扩大：先是他自己，然后是身边的门徒，最后是「那些因他们的话信我的人」（17:20），也就是今天读这一章的每一个基督徒。我们读的，是耶稣为我们所献的祷告。

深读 17:1-5「认识你独一的真神……这就是永生」

1. 「时候到了」。 「父啊，时候到了，愿你荣耀你的儿子，使儿子也荣耀你。」（17:1）从2:4「我的时候还没有到」，到12:23「人子得荣耀的时候到了」，到这里，「时候」这条线走到了终点。耶稣求父荣耀他，意思是借着十字架、复活和升天，显明他的荣耀；而这荣耀的目的，是「使儿子也荣耀你」。

2. 永生的定义。 「认识你独一的真神，并且认识你所差来的耶稣基督，这就是永生。」（17:3）这是约翰福音中唯一一处直接为「永生」下定义的经文。永生不只是时间上无限延长的生命，而是一种关系：认识神。在圣经里，「认识」不只是头脑上的知道，而是亲密的、在生命相交中的认识，耶利米书31:34应许新约中「他们从最小的到至大的都必认识我」。

3. 独一的真神与他所差来的。 这一节同时说「独一的真神」和「你所差来的耶稣基督」。耶稣在宣告一神信仰的同一句话里，把认识他自己和认识独一的真神放在一起，作为永生的内容。没有一个受造物能这样说。

4. 「已成全了」。 「我在地上已经荣耀你，你所托付我的事，我已成全了。」（17:4）十字架还没有发生，耶稣却说「已成全了」。这与16:33「我已经胜了世界」一样，是确信的语气；它也预告了十字架上的最后一句话：「成了。」（19:30）

5. 创世以前的荣耀。 「父啊，现在求你使我同你享荣耀，就是未有世界以先，我同你所有的荣耀。」（17:5）这是约翰福音对耶稣先存最清楚的宣告之一，呼应序言：「太初有道，道与神同在。」耶稣不是在求得到一份新的荣耀，而是求回到他本来就有的荣耀里，只是这一次，他是带着人性、带着被钉的伤痕回去的。

深读 17:6-19 保守与成圣

1. 「他们本是你的」。 「你从世上赐给我的人，我已将你的名显明与他们。他们本是你的，你将他们赐给我。」（17:6）门徒先是属于父的，父把他们赐给子。这呼应6:37-39：「凡父所赐给我的人必到我这里来……叫我一个也不失落。」

2. 「保守」。 「圣父啊，求你因你所赐给我的名保守他们。」（17:11）耶稣在世时亲自保守了他们（17:12），现在他要离开，就把他们交在父的手里。耶稣在这里把10:28-29「谁也不能从我父手里把他们夺去」的应许，化成了祷告。

3. 「灭亡之子」。 「其中除了那灭亡之子，没有一个灭亡的，好叫经上的话得应验。」（17:12）这指犹大。「灭亡之子」是一种闪族的表达法，意思是「注定灭亡的人」。同一个希腊词组在帖撒罗尼迦后书2:3用来描写末世的「大罪人」，和合本在那里译作「沉沦之子」。犹大的失落不是耶稣保守失败（耶稣早就知道，6:64、70），而是应验了圣经（多半指13:18所引的诗41:9）；同时，犹大仍要为自己的选择负责。

4. 在世界里，不属世界。 「我不求你叫他们离开世界，只求你保守他们脱离那恶者。」（17:15）基督徒不是要逃离世界，而是在世界里被保守。「他们不属世界，正如我不属世界一样」（17:14、16），「你怎样差我到世上，我也照样差他们到世上」（17:18）。不属世界，却被差进世界：这是门徒身份的两面。

5. 「用真理使他们成圣」。 「求你用真理使他们成圣；你的道就是真理。」（17:17）「成圣」（hagiazō）的意思是「分别出来归给神」。神用来使人成圣的工具，是他的道。不是靠离开世界，而是靠真理。

6. 「自己分别为圣」。 「我为他们的缘故，自己分别为圣，叫他们也因真理成圣。」（17:19）这里的「分别为圣」是同一个字 hagiazō。在旧约里，这个字用于祭司被分别出来（出28:41），也用于献给神的祭物（申15:19「都要分别为圣，归耶和华」）。耶稣说这话时，正走向十字架：他把自己分别出来作祭物，好叫门徒可以被分别出来归给神。这也呼应10:36：「父所分别为圣、又差到世间来的。」

深读 17:20-23「使他们都合而为一」

1. 为我们祷告。 「我不但为这些人祈求，也为那些因他们的话信我的人祈求。」（17:20）今天每一个因为使徒所传、所写的话而信主的人，都在这个祷告之中。

2. 合一的样式。 「使他们都合而为一。正如你父在我里面，我在你里面，使他们也在我们里面。」（17:21）门徒合一的样式，是父与子的合一；门徒合一的基础，是「在我们里面」，也就是与神的联合。这不首先是组织上的统一，而是生命上的合一。

3. 合一的目的。 「叫世人可以信你差了我来。」（17:21）又说：「叫世人知道你差了我来，也知道你爱他们如同爱我一样。」（17:23）基督徒的合一本身就是福音的见证（参13:35）。分裂与纷争（包括为面子、为人事而起的纷争），会让世界看不见基督。

4. 在真理中的合一。 这个合一不能脱离前面的祷告：「求你用真理使他们成圣。」（17:17）耶稣所求的合一，是在他的道、他的真理中的合一，不是以放弃真理为代价的合一。但同样，真理也不能成为不合一的借口。

要点：耶稣在被出卖的那个晚上，为今天的我们祷告：愿我们被父保守，被真理分别为圣，在他里面合而为一，叫世人可以信。
深读 17:24-26「叫他们看见你所赐给我的荣耀」

1. 耶稣的心愿。 「父啊，我在哪里，愿你所赐给我的人也同我在那里，叫他们看见你所赐给我的荣耀。」（17:24）「愿」（thelō）是一个很强的字，与前面的「求」（9、15、20节）相比，这是子对父直接表达的心愿。耶稣最深的心愿之一，是我们与他同在，看见他的荣耀。这呼应14:3：「我在哪里，叫你们也在那里。」

2. 创立世界以前的爱。 「因为创立世界以前，你已经爱我了。」（17:24）在有任何受造物之前，父与子之间就有永恒的爱。神不是因为孤单才创造人；他在永恒中就是爱（约壹4:8）。而这爱，耶稣要让它「在他们里面」（17:26）。

3. 结语。 「我已将你的名指示他们，还要指示他们，使你所爱我的爱在他们里面，我也在他们里面。」（17:26）祷告结束在爱和内住：父爱子的那份爱，要在门徒里面；而子自己，也要在他们里面。祷告完了，耶稣就出去，过了汲沦溪，走进园子（18:1）。

默想

默想： 耶稣说永生就是「认识你」。我对神的认识，是停留在知道关于他的事，还是真的在与他相交、认识他自己？在世界里、却不属世界：我在哪一方面太像世界，又在哪一方面太远离我被差去的地方？耶稣在被卖的那夜为我祷告，他最深的心愿是我与他同在、看见他的荣耀。被这样爱着，我愿意怎样去爱那个与我最难合一的弟兄姊妹？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 17 is the longest recorded prayer of Jesus in the New Testament. The Upper Room Discourse is over; Jesus "lifted up his eyes to heaven," and the disciples listen as he speaks with the Father. Sixteenth-century Lutheran theologians (the title is usually credited to David Chytraeus) called it "the high-priestly prayer," because here, like a high priest, Jesus intercedes for his people before offering himself. Jesus prays for himself (vv. 1–5): "glorify your Son." For his disciples (vv. 6–19): "keep them... sanctify them in the truth." For future believers (vv. 20–26): "that they may all be one."

The prayer widens in circles: first Jesus himself, then the disciples around him, and finally "those who will believe in me through their word" (17:20), which means every Christian reading this chapter today. What we're reading is Jesus' prayer for us.

Going Deeper: 17:1–5 "That they know you, the only true God... this is eternal life"

1. "The hour has come." "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you" (17:1). From "My hour has not yet come" (2:4) to "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified" (12:23) to here, the thread of the "hour" reaches its end. Jesus asks the Father to glorify him, meaning to reveal his glory through the cross, resurrection and ascension, and the purpose of that glory is "that the Son may glorify you."

2. Eternal life defined. "And this is eternal life, that they know you the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent" (17:3). This is the only verse in John that directly defines eternal life. Eternal life isn't merely life extended forever; it's a relationship: knowing God. In Scripture, "knowing" isn't only head knowledge but intimate, relational knowledge. Jeremiah 31:34 promises that in the new covenant "they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest."

3. The Son within monotheism. This verse speaks of "the only true God" and "Jesus Christ whom you have sent" together. In the same sentence that confesses one God, Jesus places knowing himself alongside knowing the only true God as the content of eternal life. No creature could say that.

4. "Having accomplished." "I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do" (17:4). The cross hasn't happened yet, but Jesus speaks of the work as accomplished. Like "I have overcome the world" (16:33), it's the language of certainty, and it anticipates his last word from the cross: "It is finished" (19:30).

5. Glory before the world existed. "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed" (17:5). This is one of John's clearest statements of Jesus' pre-existence, echoing the Prologue: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God." Jesus isn't asking for a new glory but to return to the glory he always had, only this time returning with his humanity and the scars of the cross.

Going Deeper: 17:6–19 Kept and Sanctified

1. "Yours they were." "I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me" (17:6). The disciples first belonged to the Father, who gave them to the Son. This echoes 6:37–39: "All that the Father gives me will come to me... that I should lose nothing."

2. "Keep them." "Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me" (17:11). On earth Jesus kept them himself (17:12); now that he is leaving, he entrusts them to the Father's hands. This is the prayer form of 10:28–29, "no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand."

3. "The son of destruction." "Not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled" (17:12). This refers to Judas. "Son of destruction" is a Semitic expression meaning "one destined for destruction." The same Greek phrase is used in 2 Thessalonians 2:3 of the end-time "man of lawlessness," where the ESV renders it "the son of destruction" too. Judas's loss isn't a failure of Jesus' keeping (Jesus knew from the start, 6:64, 70) but the fulfillment of Scripture (probably Ps 41:9, quoted at 13:18); at the same time, Judas remains responsible for his choice.

4. In the world, not of it. "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one" (17:15). Christians aren't meant to escape the world but to be kept within it. "They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world" (17:14, 16), and "As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world" (17:18). Not of the world, yet sent into it: these are the two sides of a disciple's identity.

5. "Sanctify them in the truth." "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth" (17:17). "Sanctify" (hagiazō) means to set apart for God. The tool God uses to sanctify people is his word. Not by leaving the world, but by the truth.

6. "I consecrate myself." "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth" (17:19). "Consecrate" is the same word, hagiazō. In the Old Testament it was used for priests being set apart (Ex 28:41) and for offerings dedicated to God (Deut 15:19, "you shall dedicate to the LORD your God"). Jesus says this as he walks toward the cross: he sets himself apart as the sacrifice so that the disciples can be set apart for God. It also echoes 10:36: "him whom the Father consecrated and sent into the world."

Going Deeper: 17:20–23 "That they may all be one"

1. A prayer for us. "I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word" (17:20). Everyone who has come to faith through what the apostles preached and wrote is included in this prayer.

2. The pattern of unity. "That they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us" (17:21). The pattern of the disciples' unity is the unity of Father and Son; its basis is "in us," union with God. This is first of all not organizational uniformity but a unity of life.

3. The purpose of unity. "So that the world may believe that you have sent me" (17:21), and, "so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me" (17:23). Christian unity is itself a witness to the gospel (cf. 13:35). Division and strife keep the world from seeing Christ.

4. Unity in the truth. This unity can't be separated from the earlier petition: "Sanctify them in the truth" (17:17). The unity Jesus prays for is unity in his word and truth, not unity bought by abandoning the truth. Equally, truth must not become an excuse for disunity.

The point: On the night he was betrayed, Jesus prayed for us today: that we would be kept by the Father, set apart by the truth, and made one in him, so that the world may believe.
Going Deeper: 17:24–26 "To see my glory"

1. Jesus' desire. "Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me" (17:24). "Desire" (thelō) is a strong word: set against "I ask" in verses 9, 15 and 20, it is the Son directly expressing his will to the Father. One of Jesus' deepest desires is that we be with him and see his glory. This echoes 14:3: "where I am you may be also."

2. Love before the foundation of the world. "Because you loved me before the foundation of the world" (17:24). Before anything was created, there was eternal love between the Father and the Son. God didn't create humanity out of loneliness; he has always been love (1 John 4:8). And this love Jesus means to be "in them" (17:26).

3. The close. "I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them" (17:26). The prayer ends with love and indwelling: the Father's love for the Son will be in the disciples, and the Son himself will be in them. When the prayer ends, Jesus goes out across the Kidron Valley into a garden (18:1).

Meditation

Reflect: Jesus says eternal life is "that they know you." Does my knowledge of God stop at knowing about him, or am I truly coming to know him? In the world but not of it: in what ways am I too much like the world, and in what ways am I too far from the place I've been sent? On the night he was betrayed Jesus prayed for me, and his deepest desire is that I be with him and see his glory. Loved like that, how might I love the brother or sister I find it hardest to be one with?
