entries.content:
本章脉络

第十三章是使徒行传的第二个起点。从这里开始，故事的中心从耶路撒冷转到安提阿，焦点从彼得转到保罗；福音也开始有计划地向「地极」推进。

本章有四段：安提阿的差遣（1-3节），圣灵在敬拜中说话，教会差出巴拿巴和扫罗；塞浦路斯（4-12节），行法术的以吕马瞎了眼，罗马方伯信了主；彼西底的安提阿（13-41节），保罗在会堂里的第一篇长篇讲道，以「称义」作为高峰；两种回应（42-52节），外邦人欢喜，犹太人嫉妒，使徒被赶出境外，门徒却「满心喜乐」。

深读 13:1-3 在敬拜中被差遣

1. 一个多元的领袖群体。 「在安提阿的教会中，有几位先知和教师，就是巴拿巴和称呼尼结的西面、古利奈人路求，与分封之王希律同养的马念，并扫罗。」（13:1）巴拿巴来自塞浦路斯；「尼结」是拉丁文「黑」的意思，西面可能来自非洲；路求来自北非的古利奈；马念是和分封之王希律安提帕一同长大的人（原文这个词也可指宫廷近臣）；扫罗是大数的法利赛人。安提阿教会的领袖，本身就是福音拆毁隔断之墙的见证。

2. 事奉主、禁食的时候。 「他们事奉主、禁食的时候，圣灵说：『要为我分派巴拿巴和扫罗，去做我召他们所做的工。』」（13:2）教会历史上第一次有计划的宣教差遣，不是从策略会议开始的，而是从敬拜和禁食中开始的。「事奉主」原文是 leitourgeō，常用来指圣殿里的敬拜事奉。

3. 「为我」分派。 圣灵说「要为我分派」：宣教士首先是属于神的，然后才是属于教会的。「我召他们」：呼召来自圣灵。可是圣灵把这个呼召交给教会去确认、去差遣：「于是禁食祷告，按手在他们头上，就打发他们去了。」（13:3）第4节说：「他们既被圣灵差遣。」差遣的，是圣灵，也是教会；两者不冲突。

4. 差出最好的。 安提阿教会差出的，不是闲着没事的人，而是他们最有恩赐的两位教师。一个愿意把最好的献出去的教会，才是真正明白福音的教会。

要点：宣教不是教会的一项活动，而是圣灵的工作；教会在敬拜中聆听，又甘心把最好的人交给神。
深读 13:4-12 塞浦路斯：方伯与行法术的人

1. 先到会堂。 他们到了撒拉米，「就在犹太人各会堂里传讲神的道」（13:5）。这是保罗一贯的做法：先向犹太人，再向外邦人（参罗1:16）。

2. 方伯士求‧保罗。 在帕弗，他们遇见罗马方伯士求‧保罗，「是个通达人」，「要听神的道」（13:7）。罗马帝国的高官，愿意听两位犹太巡回传道人讲道。

3. 以吕马的敌挡。 行法术的巴‧耶稣（又名以吕马）「敌挡使徒，要叫方伯不信真道」（13:8）。保罗「被圣灵充满，定睛看他」，说：「你这充满各样诡诈奸恶，魔鬼的儿子……你混乱主的正道还不止住吗？」（13:9-10）「巴‧耶稣」意思是「耶稣（约书亚）的儿子」，保罗却称他为「魔鬼的儿子」。「混乱主的正道」原文是「把主笔直的道路弄弯」，呼应以赛亚书「在沙漠地修平我们神的道」（赛40:3）。

4. 暂且瞎眼。 「现在主的手加在你身上，你要瞎眼，暂且不见日光。」（13:11）保罗自己曾在大马士革路上瞎眼三天，然后眼睛得开。以吕马的瞎眼是审判，但「暂且」二字，或许也留下了悔改的余地。

5. 「很希奇主的道」。 「方伯看见所做的事，很希奇主的道，就信了。」（13:12）路加说得很细：方伯看见的是神迹，希奇的却是「主的道」。神迹的作用，是叫人注意神的话。

6. 扫罗又名保罗。 「扫罗又名保罗。」（13:9）从这里开始，除了保罗自己讲述归主经历的地方（22:7，13；26:14），路加都称他为「保罗」。扫罗是他的希伯来名字，保罗是他的罗马名字。当他开始向外邦世界传福音时，路加就用这个外邦世界熟悉的名字称呼他。「巴拿巴和扫罗」也渐渐变成了「保罗和他的同人」（13:13）。

深读 13:13-41 保罗在会堂里的讲道

1. 约翰马可离开。 「约翰就离开他们，回耶路撒冷去。」（13:13）路加没有说原因。这件事后来在保罗和巴拿巴之间引起了一场严重的争执（15:37-39）。

2. 「若有什么劝勉众人的话」。 在彼西底的安提阿，管会堂的读完律法和先知书以后，请他们说话（13:15）。保罗「站起来，举手」（13:16），开始了路加为我们记录的第一篇保罗讲道。他的对象有两种人：「以色列人和一切敬畏神的人」，也就是犹太人和像哥尼流那样敬畏神的外邦人。

3. 从出埃及到大卫。 保罗先回顾以色列的历史：神拣选列祖，领他们出埃及，在旷野容忍他们，赐他们迦南地，兴起士师和扫罗王，然后「选立大卫作他们的王」（13:17-22）。他引用神的话：「我寻得耶西的儿子大卫，他是合我心意的人。」（13:22；参诗89:20；撒上13:14）

4. 从大卫到耶稣。 「从这人的后裔中，神已经照着所应许的，为以色列人立了一位救主，就是耶稣。」（13:23）整段历史都指向这一位。和司提反一样，保罗讲历史，是要讲基督；不同的是，司提反的重点是「你们弃绝了他」，保罗的重点是「神应验了应许」。

5. 不认识他，却应验了预言。 「耶路撒冷居住的人和他们的官长，因为不认识基督，也不明白每安息日所读众先知的书，就把基督定了死罪，正应了先知的预言。」（13:27）他们每个安息日都读先知书，却没有认出先知书所讲的那一位；而他们定他的罪，正好应验了他们所读的经文。

6. 三处经文证明复活。 保罗用三处经文讲耶稣的复活： - 「你是我的儿子，我今日生你」（13:33；诗2:7）。这里的「生」不是指耶稣的起源，他本是永远的神子；而是指神藉着复活，公开宣告并高举他为有能力的神子、受膏的王（参罗1:4「以大能显明是神的儿子」）。 - 「我必将所应许大卫那圣洁、可靠的恩典赐给你们」（13:34；赛55:3）。神给大卫的应许是永远的，只有一位永远活着的大卫的子孙，才能使这应许「可靠」。 - 「你必不叫你的圣者见朽坏」（13:35；诗16:10）。在七十士译本里，「圣洁……的恩典」（ta hosia）和「你的圣者」（ton hosion sou）是同一个字，所以保罗把这两处经文放在一起读。保罗的论证和彼得在五旬节的论证一样（2:25-31）：大卫「已见朽坏」，「惟独神所复活的，他并未见朽坏」（13:36-37）。

7. 讲道的高峰：称义。 「所以，弟兄们，你们当晓得：赦罪的道是由这人传给你们的。你们靠摩西的律法，在一切不得称义的事上信靠这人，就都得称义了。」（13:38-39）这是使徒行传中唯一一次出现保罗书信的核心词「称义」（dikaioō）。和合本这一句不容易读，意思是：凡靠摩西的律法在一切事上都不能称义的，信靠这人就都得称义了。这不是说律法能使人在某些事上称义、耶稣补足其余的；而是说律法在任何事上都不能使人称义，耶稣却使信他的人在一切事上称义。这正是保罗在加拉太书和罗马书里要详细展开的福音。

8. 警告。 保罗最后引用哈巴谷书：「你们这轻慢的人要观看，要惊奇，要灭亡；因为在你们的时候，我行一件事，虽有人告诉你们，你们总是不信。」（13:41；哈1:5）哈巴谷当年说的「一件事」，是神要兴起巴比伦来审判犹大（保罗的引文跟随七十士译本「你们这轻慢的人」；希伯来文本作「你们要向列国中观看」）；现在神行的「一件事」，是在耶稣里施行拯救。轻慢这救恩，比当年轻慢审判的警告更危险。

要点：保罗讲以色列的整段历史，是为了讲一个人：大卫的子孙耶稣。他的死应验了经文，他的复活证明了神的应许；凡信靠他的，律法所不能做的，他都成就了：「就都得称义了」。
深读 13:42-52 欢喜与嫉妒

1. 合城的人几乎都来了。 「到下安息日，合城的人几乎都来聚集，要听神的道。」（13:44）福音向所有人敞开的消息，吸引了整座城。

2. 满心嫉妒。 「但犹太人看见人这样多，就满心嫉妒，硬驳保罗所说的话，并且毁谤。」（13:45）他们嫉妒的，或许不只是人数，而是这些外邦人不必先成为犹太人，就可以直接蒙神接纳。

3. 「断定自己不配得永生」。 「神的道先讲给你们原是应当的；只因你们弃绝这道，断定自己不配得永生，我们就转向外邦人去。」（13:46）路加强调的是他们自己的责任：他们弃绝了道，就是「断定自己不配得永生」。

4. 外邦人的光。 「因为主曾这样吩咐我们说：我已经立你作外邦人的光，叫你施行救恩，直到地极。」（13:47；赛49:6）以赛亚书这句话原是讲「耶和华的仆人」，耶稣就是那位仆人（参路2:32，西面称耶稣为「照亮外邦人的光」）。现在保罗和巴拿巴说，这是主「吩咐我们」的：他们跟随那位仆人，也一同承担仆人的使命。

5. 「凡预定得永生的人都信了」。 「外邦人听见这话，就欢喜了，赞美神的道；凡预定得永生的人都信了。」（13:48）这节经文和第46节放在一起，就看见圣经的两面：人弃绝福音，要为自己负责（46节）；人相信福音，是因为神的预定和恩典（48节）。神的拣选不叫人骄傲，因为信心本身就是恩典；也不叫人灰心，因为福音仍然向每一个人宣讲。

6. 跺下脚上的尘土。 他们被赶出境外，「二人对着众人跺下脚上的尘土，就往以哥念去了」（13:51）。这是照着耶稣的吩咐（路9:5），表示「我们已经尽了责任，后果由你们自己承担」。

7. 满心喜乐。 「门徒满心喜乐，又被圣灵充满。」（13:52）使徒被赶走了，留下来的初信者却满心喜乐。他们的喜乐不倚靠传道人在不在，而倚靠那位住在他们里面的圣灵。

要点：同一篇讲道，有人嫉妒，有人欢喜。弃绝福音的人，是自己断定自己不配；相信福音的人，却只能把功劳归给神的预定和恩典。
默想

默想： 第一次宣教差遣，是在安提阿的教会「事奉主、禁食」的时候发生的。我常常想知道神要我做什么，却很少在敬拜和安静中等候他说话。这一周，我能不能为一个具体的决定，空出一段时间祷告，甚至禁食一餐，单单寻求他的心意？保罗说，律法所不能叫人称义的，凡信靠耶稣的「就都得称义了」。我心里是否还有一部分，在暗暗用自己的表现计算我在神面前的地位：今天读经了，就觉得神喜悦我；今天发脾气了，就觉得神远离我？在神面前，我的义已经在基督里完全成就了；我可以带着这份确据去读经、去服事，而不是为了得到它。最后，使徒被赶出城，初信的门徒却「满心喜乐，又被圣灵充满」。如果我所依靠的传道人、带领我的弟兄姊妹离开了，我的喜乐还在吗？那位住在我里面的圣灵，从来没有离开。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 13 is Acts' second starting point. From here the story's center moves from Jerusalem to Antioch, its focus from Peter to Paul, and the gospel begins a deliberate advance toward "the end of the earth."

The chapter has four parts: sending from Antioch (vv. 1–3), where the Spirit speaks in worship and the church sends out Barnabas and Saul; Cyprus (vv. 4–12), where the magician Elymas is blinded and a Roman proconsul believes; Pisidian Antioch (vv. 13–41), Paul's first long synagogue sermon, which peaks in "justification"; and two responses (vv. 42–52): Gentiles rejoice, Jews are jealous, the apostles are driven out, and the disciples are "filled with joy."

Going Deeper: 13:1–3 Sent Out in Worship

1. A diverse leadership. "Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a member of the court of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul" (13:1). Barnabas was from Cyprus; "Niger" is Latin for "black," and Simeon may have come from Africa; Lucius was from Cyrene in North Africa; Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas (the word can also mean a close member of his court); Saul was a Pharisee from Tarsus. The leadership of the Antioch church was itself a witness to the gospel breaking down dividing walls.

2. While they were worshiping and fasting. "While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them'" (13:2). The first planned missionary sending in church history didn't begin in a strategy meeting; it began in worship and fasting. "Worshiping" is leitourgeō, a word often used for the worship service of the temple.

3. Set apart "for me." The Spirit says "set apart for me": missionaries belong first to God, and only then to the church. "I have called them": the call comes from the Spirit. Yet the Spirit gives the church the task of confirming and sending: "Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off" (13:3). Verse 4 says they were "sent out by the Holy Spirit." The sending is the Spirit's and the church's; the two don't conflict.

4. Sending their best. The Antioch church didn't send people who had nothing else to do; it sent its two most gifted teachers. A church willing to give away its best is a church that has understood the gospel.

The point: Mission isn't one of the church's programs; it is the Spirit's work. The church listens in worship and gladly hands its best people to God.
Going Deeper: 13:4–12 Cyprus: The Proconsul and the Magician

1. Synagogues first. At Salamis "they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews" (13:5). This was Paul's consistent pattern: to the Jew first, and also to the Greek (cf. Rom 1:16).

2. The proconsul Sergius Paulus. At Paphos they met the Roman proconsul Sergius Paulus, "a man of intelligence," who "sought to hear the word of God" (13:7). A high Roman official was willing to listen to two traveling Jewish preachers.

3. Elymas's opposition. The magician Bar-Jesus, also called Elymas, "opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith" (13:8). Paul, "filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, 'You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?'" (13:9–10). "Bar-Jesus" means "son of Jesus (Joshua)," but Paul calls him "son of the devil." "Making crooked the straight paths" echoes Isaiah's "make straight in the desert a highway for our God" (Isa 40:3).

4. Blind for a time. "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time" (13:11). Paul himself had been blinded for three days on the Damascus road before his eyes were opened. Elymas's blindness was judgment, but "for a time" may also leave room for repentance.

5. Astonished at the teaching. "Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord" (13:12). Luke is careful: the proconsul saw a miracle, but what astonished him was "the teaching of the Lord." Miracles serve to draw attention to God's word.

6. Saul, also called Paul. "But Saul, who was also called Paul" (13:9). From here on Luke calls him "Paul," except where Paul retells his conversion (22:7, 13; 26:14). Saul was his Hebrew name and Paul his Roman name; as he begins taking the gospel into the Gentile world, Luke uses the name that world knew. "Barnabas and Saul" also gradually becomes "Paul and his companions" (13:13).

Going Deeper: 13:13–41 Paul's Synagogue Sermon

1. John Mark leaves. "And John left them and returned to Jerusalem" (13:13). Luke gives no reason. Later this would cause a sharp disagreement between Paul and Barnabas (15:37–39).

2. "Any word of exhortation." At Pisidian Antioch, after the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the synagogue rulers invited them to speak (13:15). Paul "stood up, and motioning with his hand" (13:16), began the first sermon of Paul's that Luke records for us. He addressed two groups: "Men of Israel and you who fear God," that is, Jews and God-fearing Gentiles like Cornelius.

3. From the exodus to David. Paul first reviews Israel's history: God chose the fathers, led them out of Egypt, put up with them in the wilderness, gave them Canaan, raised up judges and King Saul, and then "raised up David to be their king" (13:17–22). He quotes God's word: "I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart" (13:22; cf. Ps 89:20; 1 Sam 13:14).

4. From David to Jesus. "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised" (13:23). The whole history points to this one person. Like Stephen, Paul tells history to tell of Christ; but where Stephen's emphasis was "you rejected him," Paul's is "God has kept his promise."

5. Not recognizing him, yet fulfilling the prophets. "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him" (13:27). They read the prophets every Sabbath but didn't recognize the one the prophets spoke of; and by condemning him they fulfilled the very Scriptures they read.

6. Three Scriptures for the resurrection. Paul uses three texts to speak of Jesus' resurrection: - "You are my Son, today I have begotten you" (13:33; Ps 2:7). "Begotten" here doesn't refer to Jesus' origin, for he is the eternal Son. It refers to God publicly declaring and enthroning him, through the resurrection, as the messianic King, "the Son of God in power" (Rom 1:4). - "I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David" (13:34; Isa 55:3). God's promise to David was everlasting; only a Son of David who lives forever can make those blessings "sure." - "You will not let your Holy One see corruption" (13:35; Ps 16:10). In the Septuagint, "holy [blessings]" (ta hosia) and "your Holy One" (ton hosion sou) share one word, which is why Paul reads the two texts together. Paul's argument is the same as Peter's at Pentecost (2:25–31): David "saw corruption," "but he whom God raised up did not see corruption" (13:36–37).

7. The sermon's peak: justification. "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses" (13:38–39). "Freed" here translates dikaioō, "justify," the key word of Paul's letters, and the only place it appears in Acts. Luke is not saying the law justifies in some matters and Jesus completes the rest; the law could justify from nothing, and Jesus justifies the believer from everything. This is the gospel Paul will unfold in detail in Galatians and Romans.

8. A warning. Paul closes with Habakkuk: "Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you" (13:41; Hab 1:5). The "work" in Habakkuk's day was God raising up Babylon to judge Judah (Paul's wording, "you scoffers," follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads "Look among the nations"); the "work" God is doing now is salvation in Jesus. Scorning this salvation is more dangerous than scorning that warning of judgment.

The point: Paul tells Israel's whole history to speak of one person: Jesus, the Son of David. His death fulfilled the Scriptures, his resurrection proved God's promises, and for everyone who believes in him he has done what the law could not: they are justified.
Going Deeper: 13:42–52 Joy and Jealousy

1. Almost the whole city came. "The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord" (13:44). The news that the gospel was open to all drew the entire city.

2. Filled with jealousy. "But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him" (13:45). What provoked their jealousy may not have been only the crowd's size but the fact that these Gentiles could be accepted by God without first becoming Jews.

3. "Judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life." "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles" (13:46). Luke puts the weight on their own responsibility: by thrusting the word aside, they "judge themselves unworthy of eternal life."

4. A light for the Gentiles. "For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth'" (13:47; Isa 49:6). In Isaiah these words are spoken of "the Servant of the LORD," and Jesus is that Servant (cf. Luke 2:32, where Simeon calls Jesus "a light for revelation to the Gentiles"). Now Paul and Barnabas say the Lord has "commanded us": following the Servant, they share in the Servant's mission.

5. "As many as were appointed to eternal life believed." "And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed" (13:48). Read alongside verse 46, this shows both sides of Scripture: those who reject the gospel are responsible for doing so (v. 46); those who believe it do so because of God's appointment and grace (v. 48). God's choosing doesn't make anyone proud, since faith itself is grace; nor does it make anyone despair, since the gospel is still proclaimed to everyone.

6. Shaking off the dust. Driven out of the district, "they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium" (13:51). This followed Jesus' instruction (Luke 9:5) and meant, "We have done our duty; you bear the consequences."

7. Filled with joy. "And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit" (13:52). The apostles were driven away, yet the new believers left behind were full of joy. Their joy didn't depend on whether the preachers stayed but on the Spirit who lived in them.

The point: The same sermon drew jealousy from some and joy from others. Those who reject the gospel judge themselves unworthy; those who believe can credit only God's appointment and grace.
Meditation

Reflect: The first missionary sending happened while the church at Antioch was "worshiping the Lord and fasting." I often want to know what God wants me to do, yet rarely wait for him in worship and quiet. This week, could I set aside time to pray about one specific decision, perhaps even skipping a meal to fast, and seek his will alone? Paul said that everyone who believes in Jesus is justified, as the law could never do. Is part of me still quietly calculating my standing before God by my performance: I read my Bible today, so God must be pleased with me; I lost my temper today, so God must feel far away? Before God my righteousness is already complete in Christ; I can read and serve from that assurance, not in order to earn it. Finally, the apostles were driven out of town, yet the new disciples were "filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit." If the pastor I rely on, or the brothers and sisters who lead me, were to leave, would my joy still be there? The Spirit who lives in me has never left.

本章脉络

第十四章完成了第一次宣教旅程。以哥念（1-7节）：许多人信了，城里却分了党，使徒被迫逃走。路司得（8-20节）：一个生来瘸腿的人得医治，众人把巴拿巴和保罗当作希腊的神明，要向他们献祭；没过多久，同一群人却用石头打保罗，以为他死了。回程（21-28节）：他们回到刚刚逼迫过他们的城，坚固门徒，选立长老，然后回到差派他们的安提阿，述说「神怎样为外邦人开了信道的门」。

这一章有一个强烈的对比：人一会儿要拜他们，一会儿要杀他们。传道人若把信心建立在人的反应上，很快就会垮掉；保罗和巴拿巴所倚靠的，是那位「证明他的恩道」的主（14:3）。

深读 14:1-7 以哥念：恩道与分裂

1. 犹太人和希腊人信的很多。 「二人在以哥念同进犹太人的会堂，在那里讲的，叫犹太人和希腊人信的很多。」（14:1）福音一传开，就同时得着犹太人和外邦人。

2. 他的恩道。 「二人在那里住了多日，倚靠主放胆讲道，主藉他们的手施行神迹奇事，证明他的恩道。」（14:3）路加用一个美丽的名称称呼福音：「他的恩道」，就是关于神恩典的道。神迹在这里的作用，是「证明」这恩典的话是真的。

3. 城里的人分了党。 「城里的众人就分了党，有附从犹太人的，有附从使徒的。」（14:4）耶稣曾说，他来是要叫人「纷争」（路12:51）。福音带来平安，也带来分别。

4. 逃走，然后继续传。 有人要「用石头打他们」，「使徒知道了，就逃往吕高尼的路司得、特庇两个城和周围地方去，在那里传福音」（14:5-7）。逃避逼迫不是不忠心（参太10:23）；他们离开一个地方，只是为了在另一个地方继续传福音。

深读 14:8-18 路司得：「我们也是人」

1. 有信心可得痊愈。 路司得有一个人「生来是瘸腿的，从来没有走过」。「他听保罗讲道，保罗定睛看他，见他有信心，可得痊愈，就大声说：『你起来，两脚站直！』那人就跳起来，而且行走。」（14:8-10）这件事几乎和彼得在圣殿美门口医治瘸腿的人一模一样（3:1-10）。路加有意让我们看见：在外邦人中工作的保罗，和在犹太人中工作的彼得，是同一位主所用的。

2. 神藉着人形降临。 众人用本地的吕高尼话大喊：「有神藉着人形降临在我们中间了。」（14:11）他们称巴拿巴为宙斯，称保罗为希耳米，「因为他说话领首」（14:12）。罗马诗人奥维德记载过一个传说（腓利门与巴乌西斯）：宙斯和希耳米化成人形来到邻近的弗吕家，无人接待，只有一对贫穷的老夫妇款待了他们，其余的人都遭了灾。当地也出土过同时敬拜这两位神明的碑文。路司得人也许知道类似的传说，不想再犯同样的错误。

3. 撕开衣裳。 宙斯庙的祭司牵着牛、拿着花圈要献祭，「巴拿巴、保罗二使徒听见，就撕开衣裳，跳进众人中间」（14:13-14）。撕开衣裳，是犹太人听见亵渎神的话时的反应。对他们来说，被人当作神来敬拜，不是荣耀，而是可怕的亵渎。

4. 「我们也是人，性情和你们一样。」 「诸君，为什么做这事呢？我们也是人，性情和你们一样。我们传福音给你们，是叫你们离弃这些虚妄，归向那创造天、地、海，和其中万物的永生神。」（14:15）对这些不认识旧约的外邦人，保罗不是从摩西和大卫讲起，而是从创造主讲起。这是向没有圣经背景的人传福音的第一个例子，到第十七章雅典的讲道会更完整。

5. 神为自己留下的证据。 「他在从前的世代，任凭万国各行其道；然而为自己未尝不显出证据来，就如常施恩惠，从天降雨，赏赐丰年，叫你们饮食饱足，满心喜乐。」（14:16-17）神学上称这为「普遍恩典」：神赐雨水和丰收给所有人，不论他们是否认识他。保罗在罗马书说，神的永能和神性「藉着所造之物就可以晓得，叫人无可推诿」（罗1:20）。每一碗饭、每一场雨，都在为神作见证。这样的见证足以叫人无可推诿，却不足以叫人得救；所以保罗还要传福音，叫他们「离弃这些虚妄，归向」永生神（14:15）。

6. 仅仅拦住。 「二人说了这些话，仅仅地拦住众人不献祭与他们。」（14:18）人心多么容易拜偶像：就在使徒面前，他们还几乎要把使徒当成偶像。

要点：路司得人不认识真神，就把行神迹的人当作神。保罗不肯接受这份荣耀，却把他们指向那位一直藉着雨水和丰收向他们施恩的创造主。
深读 14:19-20 被石头打，又起来

1. 同一群人。 「但有些犹太人从安提阿和以哥念来，挑唆众人，就用石头打保罗，以为他是死了，便拖到城外。」（14:19）不久前还要向他献祭的人，现在要用石头打死他。人的赞美和人的愤怒，常常只隔着一点点距离。

2. 保罗记得这件事。 保罗后来说：「被石头打了一次。」（林后11:25）他也写信给提摩太，提到「我在安提阿、以哥念、路司得所遭遇的逼迫、苦难」，又说「从这一切苦难中，主都把我救出来了」（提后3:11）。提摩太就是路司得人（16:1）；他很可能亲眼看见了这件事。

3. 他就起来，走进城去。 「门徒正围着他，他就起来，走进城去。第二天，同巴拿巴往特庇去。」（14:20）路加没有说这是神迹，但这个画面很有力量：被石头打得像死了一样的人，站起来，走回打他的那座城。

深读 14:21-28 回程：坚固、劝勉、交托

1. 原路回去。 在特庇传福音以后，他们「就回路司得、以哥念、安提阿去」（14:21）。解经家常指出，从特庇往东经过保罗的家乡大数，是回去最近的路；他们却选择往回走，回到刚刚逼迫他们的城。为什么？为了那些初信的门徒。

2. 「必须经历许多艰难」。 他们「坚固门徒的心，劝他们恒守所信的道；又说：『我们进入神的国，必须经历许多艰难。』」（14:22）这句话很诚实。保罗没有对初信的人说「信了主，一切都会顺利」，而是说艰难是「必须」的。「必须」这个字（dei），路加常用来讲神的计划（参路24:26，和合本译作「应当」：「基督这样受害，又进入他的荣耀，岂不是应当的吗？」）。艰难是进国的路，不是进国的代价；门徒所走的路，是他们的主先走过的路。

3. 选立长老。 「二人在各教会中选立了长老，又禁食祷告，就把他们交托所信的主。」（14:23）这些教会成立不久，保罗和巴拿巴就为他们选立领袖。他相信，即使没有使徒在场，主也能保守他的教会。

4. 交托所信的主。 「就把他们交托所信的主」：保罗没有把这些教会看作是他自己的。他尽了责任，然后放手，把他们交在主的手里。

5. 神为外邦人开了信道的门。 回到叙利亚的安提阿，「就述说神藉他们所行的一切事，并神怎样为外邦人开了信道的门」（14:27）。请注意主语：不是「我们为外邦人开了门」，而是「神」。他们所报告的，是神的作为。

要点：保罗和巴拿巴没有隐瞒艰难，也没有把初信的人留给自己掌管；他们说出实话，选立长老，然后把一切交托给主。
默想

默想： 路司得人先是要向保罗献祭，不久却用石头打他。我是否太在意别人对我的看法，以致被称赞时飘飘然，被批评时就一蹶不振？保罗的稳定，来自他知道自己「也是人」，也知道那位创造天地的永生神是谁。保罗对外邦人说，神「从天降雨，赏赐丰年，叫你们饮食饱足，满心喜乐」。我今天吃的每一顿饭，是否都让我想起那位赐食物的神？许多华人吃饭前会说「感谢老天爷」，却不认识那位真正赐雨水的主；我能不能在今天的饭桌上，向家人说出那位赐恩者的名字？最后，保罗对初信的人说：「我们进入神的国，必须经历许多艰难。」然后「把他们交托所信的主」。在我的生命中，有没有一个我很牵挂的人：一个将要离家的孩子，一位刚信主的朋友，一个我带过的小组？我已经尽了我能尽的；今天，我能不能把他交托在那位比我更爱他的主手里？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 14 completes the first missionary journey. Iconium (vv. 1–7): many believe, but the city is divided and the apostles have to flee. Lystra (vv. 8–20): a man crippled from birth is healed, and the crowds take Barnabas and Paul for Greek gods and try to offer sacrifices to them; soon after, the same crowds stone Paul and leave him for dead. The journey home (vv. 21–28): they go back to the very cities that had just persecuted them, strengthen the disciples, appoint elders, and return to Antioch, which had sent them, to report "how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles."

The chapter turns on a sharp contrast: one moment people want to worship them, the next they want to kill them. A preacher who builds his confidence on people's reactions will soon collapse; Paul and Barnabas relied on the Lord "who bore witness to the word of his grace" (14:3).

Going Deeper: 14:1–7 Iconium: The Word of Grace and Division

1. Many Jews and Greeks believed. "Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed" (14:1). As soon as the gospel spread, it won both Jews and Gentiles.

2. The word of his grace. "So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands" (14:3). Luke gives the gospel a beautiful name: "the word of his grace," the message about God's grace. The signs here serve to "bear witness" that this word of grace is true.

3. The city was divided. "But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles" (14:4). Jesus had said he came to bring "division" (Luke 12:51). The gospel brings peace, and it also divides.

4. Fleeing, and preaching on. When there was an attempt "to mistreat them and to stone them, they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel" (14:5–7). Escaping persecution isn't unfaithfulness (cf. Matt 10:23); they left one place only to keep preaching in another.

Going Deeper: 14:8–18 Lystra: "We Also Are Men"

1. Faith to be made well. At Lystra there was a man "crippled from birth" who "had never walked." "He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, said in a loud voice, 'Stand upright on your feet.' And he sprang up and began walking" (14:8–10). It closely mirrors Peter healing the lame man at the temple's Beautiful Gate (3:1–10). Luke wants us to see that Paul among the Gentiles and Peter among the Jews are used by the same Lord.

2. Gods in the likeness of men. The crowds shouted in their local Lycaonian language, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" (14:11). They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, "because he was the chief speaker" (14:12). The Roman poet Ovid preserves a legend (Baucis and Philemon) in which Zeus and Hermes visited neighboring Phrygia in human form; no one welcomed them except a poor elderly couple, and the rest were destroyed. Inscriptions from the area also link the two gods. The Lystrans may have known a similar story and not wanted to make the same mistake.

3. Tearing their garments. The priest of Zeus brought oxen and garlands to offer sacrifice, but "when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd" (14:13–14). Tearing one's garments was the Jewish response to hearing blasphemy. To them, being worshiped as gods was no honor but a dreadful blasphemy.

4. "We also are men, of like nature with you." "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them" (14:15). For these Gentiles who didn't know the Old Testament, Paul doesn't start with Moses and David but with the Creator. This is the first example of preaching to people with no biblical background; the Athens sermon in chapter 17 will develop it more fully.

5. The witness God left himself. "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness" (14:16–17). Theologians call this "common grace": God gives rain and harvest to everyone, whether or not they know him. In Romans Paul says God's eternal power and divine nature "have been clearly perceived... in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse" (Rom 1:20). Every bowl of rice and every rainfall bears witness to God. This witness leaves people without excuse, but it cannot save them; that is why Paul still brings "good news" calling them to "turn... to a living God" (14:15).

6. Scarcely restrained. "Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them" (14:18). How easily the human heart turns to idols: right in front of the apostles, they nearly made the apostles themselves into idols.

The point: Not knowing the true God, the people of Lystra took the miracle-workers for gods. Paul refused that glory and pointed them instead to the Creator who had been showing them kindness all along through rain and harvest.
Going Deeper: 14:19–20 Stoned, and Rising Again

1. The same crowd. "But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead" (14:19). The people who had wanted to sacrifice to him now wanted to stone him to death. Human praise and human rage are often only a short step apart.

2. Paul remembered. Paul later wrote, "Once I was stoned" (2 Cor 11:25). He also wrote to Timothy of "my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra," adding, "yet from them all the Lord rescued me" (2 Tim 3:11). Timothy was from Lystra (16:1); he may well have seen it happen.

3. He rose up and entered the city. "But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe" (14:20). Luke doesn't call it a miracle, but the picture is powerful: a man stoned until he looked dead stands up and walks back into the city that stoned him.

Going Deeper: 14:21–28 The Return: Strengthening, Encouraging, Entrusting

1. Back the way they came. After preaching in Derbe, "they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch" (14:21). Commentators often note that from Derbe the shortest way home lay east, through Paul's hometown of Tarsus; instead they went back, to the very cities that had just persecuted them. Why? For the sake of the new disciples.

2. "Through many tribulations." They were "strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God" (14:22). This is honest. Paul didn't tell new believers, "Believe in the Lord and everything will go well"; he said hardship "must" come. Luke often uses this "must" for God's plan (dei; cf. Luke 24:26, "Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?"). Tribulation is the road into the kingdom, not its price; the disciples' road is the road their Lord walked first.

3. Appointing elders. "And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed" (14:23). These churches were young, yet Paul and Barnabas appointed leaders for them. They trusted that the Lord could keep his church even without an apostle present.

4. Committed to the Lord. "They committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed": Paul didn't treat these churches as his own. He did his part, then let go and placed them in the Lord's hands.

5. God opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. Back in Syrian Antioch, "they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles" (14:27). Notice the subject: not "we opened a door for the Gentiles" but "God." What they reported was God's work.

The point: Paul and Barnabas didn't hide the hardships, nor keep the new believers under their own control. They told the truth, appointed elders, and entrusted everything to the Lord.
Meditation

Reflect: The people of Lystra first wanted to offer sacrifices to Paul; soon after, they stoned him. Do I care so much about what others think of me that praise makes me giddy and criticism flattens me? Paul's steadiness came from knowing he was "also a man," and from knowing who the living God, the Maker of heaven and earth, is. Paul told the Gentiles that God gives "rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Does each meal I eat today remind me of the God who provides it? Many Chinese people thank "Heaven" before a meal without knowing the Lord who actually sends the rain; could I name that Giver at my table today, with my family? Finally, Paul told the new believers, "Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God," and then "committed them to the Lord." Is there someone I carry on my heart: a child about to leave home, a friend newly come to faith, a small group I've led? I have done what I can; today, can I entrust them into the hands of the Lord who loves them more than I do?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第十五章接近使徒行传的中间，许多人认为这是全书神学上最关键的一章。外邦人大量归主以后，一个问题再也回避不了：外邦人要得救，是否必须先受割礼、遵守摩西的律法？换句话说：人得救，是靠「耶稣加上别的」，还是单单靠耶稣的恩典？

本章有四段：争论的起因（1-5节）；耶路撒冷会议（6-21节），彼得、巴拿巴和保罗、雅各先后发言；会议的书信（22-35节），外邦教会读了信「就欢喜了」；保罗和巴拿巴分开（36-41节），两位同工因为马可的事起了争论，各自出发。这一章既有教会最清楚的教义决定，也有同工之间最真实的冲突。

深读 15:1-5 「若不受割礼，不能得救」

1. 从犹太下来的人。 「有几个人从犹太下来，教训弟兄们说：『你们若不按摩西的规条受割礼，不能得救。』」（15:1）他们不是说「受割礼会更好」，而是说「不受割礼，不能得救」。这把割礼变成了得救的条件。

2. 大大地纷争辩论。 「保罗、巴拿巴与他们大大地纷争辩论。」（15:2）保罗没有为了表面的和睦而让步；若在这里让步，福音就不再是福音了。保罗在加拉太书中，也把类似的争论称为「福音的真理」的问题（加2:5）。加拉太书第2章所记的耶路撒冷之行，究竟是指这次会议，还是指11:30的赈灾之行，福音派学者看法不一；但两处的立场完全一致：外邦人不必受割礼，单凭恩典称义。

3. 法利赛教门的信徒。 在耶路撒冷，「有几个信徒是法利赛教门的人，起来说：『必须给外邦人行割礼，吩咐他们遵守摩西的律法。』」（15:5）请注意，他们是「信徒」。这场争论不是教会和外人的争论，而是教会内部的争论。

要点：问题不在于割礼本身，而在于把任何东西加在基督身上，作为得救的条件。「耶稣加上别的」，就不再是福音。
深读 15:6-12 彼得：「我们得救乃是因主耶稣的恩」

1. 辩论已经多了。 「使徒和长老聚会商议这事。辩论已经多了，彼得就起来。」（15:6-7）教会没有回避辩论；有分歧的时候，他们聚在一起，公开讨论。

2. 神并不分他们我们。 彼得提醒大家哥尼流家里发生的事：「知道人心的神也为他们作了见证，赐圣灵给他们，正如给我们一样；又藉着信洁净了他们的心，并不分他们我们。」（15:8-9）神已经用行动作了决定：外邦人的心是「藉着信」洁净的，不是藉着割礼。

3. 不能负的轭。 「现在为什么试探神，要把我们祖宗和我们所不能负的轭放在门徒的颈项上呢？」（15:10）这是一个犹太使徒很诚实的承认：律法本身是圣洁的（罗7:12），但作为得救之路，它是「我们祖宗和我们所不能负的轭」。没有人能靠遵守律法站在神面前。耶稣却说：「我的轭是容易的，我的担子是轻省的。」（太11:30）

4. 「和他们一样」。 「我们得救乃是因主耶稣的恩，和他们一样，这是我们所信的。」（15:11）请注意彼得的说法。他没有说「外邦人得救是因恩典，和我们一样」，而是倒过来说：「我们（犹太人）得救是因恩典，和他们（外邦人）一样。」犹太人并没有比外邦人多一条得救的路。在恩典面前，人人站在同一个地方。

5. 众人都默默无声。 「众人都默默无声，听巴拿巴和保罗述说神藉他们在外邦人中所行的神迹奇事。」（15:12）巴拿巴和保罗没有提出新的论证，只是述说神的作为。

要点：犹太人和外邦人得救，都是「因主耶稣的恩」，没有第二条路。律法是人所不能负的轭；恩典却是神白白的礼物。
深读 15:13-21 雅各：经文与智慧

1. 主的兄弟雅各。 「他们住了声，雅各就说：『诸位弟兄，请听我的话。』」（15:13）这位雅各是耶稣的兄弟，耶路撒冷教会的领袖，后来的教会传统记得他是一位严守律法的人。由他来作总结，分量特别重。

2. 阿摩司书的预言。 雅各引用阿摩司书：「此后，我要回来，重新修造大卫倒塌的帐幕……叫余剩的人，就是凡称为我名下的外邦人，都寻求主。」（15:16-17；摩9:11-12）神应许要恢复大卫的国度，而这个恢复，正包括外邦人归向神。雅各的引文跟随希腊文的七十士译本；希伯来文本作「使以色列人得以东所余剩的和所有称为我名下的国」。两种文本都指向同一件事：大卫的国度恢复的时候，列国要归入神的名下。

3. 「不可难为」。 「所以据我的意见，不可难为那归服神的外邦人。」（15:19）结论很清楚：外邦人不必受割礼，不必成为犹太人。

4. 四件事。 「只要写信，吩咐他们禁戒偶像的污秽和奸淫，并勒死的牲畜和血。」（15:20）这四件事不是得救的条件（第11节已经说清楚了）；其中关于饮食的几件，是为了让外邦信徒和犹太信徒能够在一起生活、一同吃饭。这几件事大多是犹太人最敏感的地方，有些也和利未记17-18章对「寄居的外人」的要求相似。雅各接着说：「因为从古以来，摩西的书在各城有人传讲。」（15:21）意思是：各城都有犹太人，外邦信徒要顾及他们的良心。

5. 奸淫为什么也在其中？ 其他几件主要和饮食、祭祀有关，奸淫却直接是道德问题。这里的「奸淫」（porneia）很可能包括利未记18章所禁止的各样性关系；在外邦世界，这类事极为普遍，也常和拜偶像的宴席连在一起。前三件是为了体贴犹太弟兄的良心；禁戒奸淫却是神对一切信徒永不改变的命令（林前6:18；帖前4:3）。

要点：耶路撒冷会议守住了两件事：在得救的事上，单单靠恩典，绝不妥协；在可以自由的事上，为了爱弟兄，甘心放下自己的自由；在神的道德命令上，则一同顺服。
深读 15:22-35 「圣灵和我们」

1. 一封信和两位使者。 「使徒和长老并全教会定意」，差派犹大和西拉，带着书信同保罗、巴拿巴往安提阿去（15:22-23）。他们不只寄一封信，还差人亲自去解释。

2. 「圣灵和我们定意」。 「因为圣灵和我们定意不将别的重担放在你们身上，惟有几件事是不可少的。」（15:28）这句话很特别：教会在讨论、见证神的作为、查考经文以后作出的决定，他们相信也是圣灵的意思。这是使徒时代的决定，已经成为圣经的一部分；今天教会的决定却会出错，必须时时用圣经来检验。但当教会谦卑顺服神的话、彼此商议时，可以信靠圣灵的带领。

3. 就欢喜了。 「众人念了，因为信上安慰的话就欢喜了。」（15:31）外邦信徒最怕听到的，是「你还不够」；他们收到的信，却告诉他们：在基督里，你已经完全被接纳了。

深读 15:36-41 保罗和巴拿巴分开

1. 为马可起争论。 保罗提议回去看望各城的弟兄，「巴拿巴有意要带称呼马可的约翰同去；但保罗因为马可从前在旁非利亚离开他们，不和他们同去做工，就以为不可带他去」（15:37-38）。两人都有道理：保罗看重工作的需要，巴拿巴看重马可这个人。巴拿巴是马可的表兄（西4:10），自然更愿意再给他一次机会。

2. 「甚至彼此分开」。 「于是二人起了争论，甚至彼此分开。」（15:39）「争论」原文是很强烈的字，指激烈的冲突。圣经没有替任何一方掩饰：刚刚帮助教会解决了最大分歧的两个人，自己却因为一个人选问题分开了。

3. 神仍然掌权。 结果，一个宣教队变成了两个：「巴拿巴带着马可，坐船往塞浦路斯去；保罗拣选了西拉，也出去，蒙弟兄们把他交于主的恩中。」（15:39-40）神没有因为他们的冲突而停止工作。这不是说冲突是好事，而是说神的恩典比人的软弱更大。

4. 后来的和好。 多年以后，保罗在书信中提到马可，吩咐教会「接待他」（西4:10），又说「他在传道的事上于我有益处」（提后4:11）。曾经半途离开的马可，后来成了保罗的同工，早期教父帕皮亚说他记下了彼得的讲道，传统上也认为他就是马可福音的作者。巴拿巴给马可的第二次机会，并没有白费。

要点：同一章里，教会在教义上达成了合一，两位领袖却在人事上分开了。圣经不掩饰神仆人的软弱；但神的工作没有停，马可也没有被放弃。
默想

默想： 「你们若不受割礼，不能得救。」今天，很少人会这样说；可是我心里会不会有一个类似的「若不」：若不每天灵修、若不参加某种聚会、若不守某些属灵规矩，就不算真正的基督徒？彼得说：「我们得救乃是因主耶稣的恩，和他们一样。」在恩典面前，我和我最看不上的那位信徒站在同一个地方。我能否放下那份「我比较好」的感觉，单单为同一份恩典感恩？耶路撒冷会议也提醒我，在得救的事上不能妥协，在生活的事上却可以为了爱而让步。有没有一件事，在神面前我原本有自由去做，可是为了不绊倒身边的弟兄姊妹，我愿意暂时放下？最后，马可曾经半途离开，后来却成了「在传道的事上有益处」的人。我是否因为过去的一次退缩或失败，就认定自己永远不能被神使用？那位没有放弃马可的主，今天也可以重新使用我。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 15 stands near the center of Acts, and many regard it as the book's most important chapter theologically. Once Gentiles were coming to faith in large numbers, one question could no longer be avoided: must Gentiles first be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved? In other words, are people saved by "Jesus plus something else," or by the grace of Jesus alone?

The chapter has four parts: the dispute arises (vv. 1–5); the Jerusalem council (vv. 6–21), where Peter, Barnabas and Paul, and James speak in turn; the council's letter (vv. 22–35), which the Gentile church reads and "rejoiced"; and Paul and Barnabas part ways (vv. 36–41), as the two co-workers clash over Mark and set out separately. The chapter holds both the church's clearest doctrinal decision and its most honest conflict between co-workers.

Going Deeper: 15:1–5 "Unless You Are Circumcised, You Cannot Be Saved"

1. Men from Judea. "But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, 'Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved'" (15:1). They weren't saying circumcision would be better; they were saying that without it you cannot be saved. That turns circumcision into a condition of salvation.

2. No small dissension. "Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them" (15:2). Paul didn't give way for the sake of surface harmony; give way here, and the gospel would no longer be the gospel. In Galatians Paul calls a similar dispute a matter of "the truth of the gospel" (Gal 2:5). Evangelical scholars differ on whether the Jerusalem visit of Galatians 2 is this council or the famine visit of 11:30, but the stance is the same in both: Gentiles need not be circumcised; justification is by grace alone.

3. Believers from the Pharisees. In Jerusalem, "some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses'" (15:5). Notice they were "believers." This wasn't a dispute between the church and outsiders but within the church.

The point: The issue isn't circumcision itself; it is adding anything to Christ as a condition of salvation. "Jesus plus something" is no longer the gospel.
Going Deeper: 15:6–12 Peter: "We Will Be Saved Through the Grace of the Lord Jesus"

1. Much debate. "The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up" (15:6–7). The church didn't avoid debate; when they disagreed, they met and discussed it openly.

2. No distinction between us and them. Peter reminded them of what happened in Cornelius's house: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith" (15:8–9). God had already decided by his actions: Gentile hearts were cleansed "by faith," not by circumcision.

3. A yoke we could not bear. "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?" (15:10). This is a strikingly honest admission from a Jewish apostle: the law itself is holy (Rom 7:12), but as a way to stand before God it is a yoke "neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear." No one can stand before God by keeping the law. But Jesus said, "My yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Matt 11:30).

4. "Just as they will." "But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will" (15:11). Notice how Peter puts it. He doesn't say, "Gentiles are saved by grace, just as we are," but the reverse: "We (Jews) are saved by grace, just as they (Gentiles) are." Jews have no second road to salvation. Before grace, everyone stands in the same place.

5. All fell silent. "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles" (15:12). Barnabas and Paul offered no new argument; they simply told what God had done.

The point: Jews and Gentiles alike are saved "through the grace of the Lord Jesus"; there is no other road. The law is a yoke no one can bear; grace is God's free gift.
Going Deeper: 15:13–21 James: Scripture and Wisdom

1. James the Lord's brother. "After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me'" (15:13). This James was Jesus' brother, leader of the Jerusalem church, remembered in later tradition for his strict observance of the law. A summary from him carried special weight.

2. Amos's prophecy. James quotes Amos: "After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen... that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name" (15:16–17; Amos 9:11–12). God promised to restore David's kingdom, and that restoration includes the Gentiles turning to God. James's quotation follows the Greek Septuagint; the Hebrew text reads "that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name." Both point to the same thing: when David's kingdom is restored, the nations will come under God's name.

3. "We should not trouble them." "Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God" (15:19). The conclusion is clear: Gentiles need not be circumcised or become Jews.

4. Four things. "But should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood" (15:20). These four aren't conditions of salvation (verse 11 has settled that); the food rules among them are so that Gentile and Jewish believers can live together and share meals. Most of them touched Jewish sensitivities most deeply, and several resemble what Leviticus 17–18 required of "the stranger who sojourns" among Israel. James adds, "For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him" (15:21): there are Jews in every city, and Gentile believers should be mindful of their consciences.

5. Why sexual immorality? The others mainly concern food and sacrifice, but sexual immorality is directly a moral matter. Porneia here probably covers the sexual relations forbidden in Leviticus 18, which were common in the Gentile world and often tied to idol feasts. The food rules served a brother's conscience; abstaining from sexual immorality is God's unchanging command for every believer (1 Cor 6:18; 1 Thess 4:3).

The point: The Jerusalem council held two things together: on salvation, grace alone, with no compromise; in matters of freedom, a willingness to set it aside out of love; in God's moral commands, shared obedience.
Going Deeper: 15:22–35 "The Holy Spirit and Us"

1. A letter and two messengers. "It seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church," to send Judas and Silas with a letter, along with Paul and Barnabas, to Antioch (15:22–23). They didn't only send a letter; they sent people to explain it in person.

2. "It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us." "For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements" (15:28). This is remarkable: a decision reached after debate, testimony to God's work and the Scriptures, they believed was also the Spirit's will. This apostolic decision is now part of Scripture. Church decisions today can err and must be tested by Scripture; yet when a church humbly submits to God's word and confers together, it may trust the Spirit's leading.

3. They rejoiced. "And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement" (15:31). What Gentile believers most feared to hear was "You're not enough yet"; the letter they received told them that in Christ they were fully accepted.

Going Deeper: 15:36–41 Paul and Barnabas Part Ways

1. A dispute over Mark. Paul proposed revisiting the brothers in each city. "Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work" (15:37–38). Both had a point: Paul weighed the needs of the work, Barnabas weighed Mark as a person. Barnabas was Mark's cousin (Col 4:10), and naturally more willing to give him another chance.

2. "So that they separated." "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other" (15:39). "Sharp disagreement" is a strong word for a heated conflict. Scripture covers for neither side: the two men who had just helped the church settle its greatest dispute parted ways over a personnel question.

3. God still reigns. The result was that one mission team became two: "Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord" (15:39–40). God didn't stop working because of their conflict. That doesn't make conflict good; it means God's grace is greater than human weakness.

4. Reconciliation later. Years later Paul mentions Mark in his letters, telling a church to "welcome him" (Col 4:10) and saying "he is very useful to me for ministry" (2 Tim 4:11). The Mark who once turned back became Paul's co-worker, and the early church father Papias says he recorded Peter's preaching; tradition holds he wrote the Gospel of Mark. The second chance Barnabas gave him was not wasted.

The point: In the same chapter the church reached unity on doctrine, while two leaders parted over people. Scripture doesn't hide the weakness of God's servants; but God's work didn't stop, and Mark wasn't given up on.
Meditation

Reflect: "Unless you are circumcised, you cannot be saved." Few people would say that today; but might there be a similar "unless" in my heart: unless you have devotions every day, unless you attend a certain kind of meeting, unless you keep certain spiritual rules, you're not really a Christian? Peter said, "We will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will." Before grace, I stand in the same place as the believer I think least of. Can I let go of the feeling that "I'm better" and simply give thanks for the same grace? The Jerusalem council also reminds me that I can't compromise on salvation, yet in daily life I can give way out of love. Is there something I'm free before God to do, which I'm willing to set aside for now so as not to trip up a brother or sister near me? Finally, Mark once turned back halfway, yet later became "very useful for ministry." Have I decided that because of one retreat or failure in my past, God can never use me again? The Lord who didn't give up on Mark can use me again today.
